maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is from one of the officials of a great corporation, and tells of the wonderful services the Prime Minister rendered labour. The letter is dated October 7, 1919. My object in drawing these matters to the attention of the house is to point out that the right hon. gentleman frequently leaves himself open to misinterpretation. Is it not reasonable to infer when we have a statement of credentials covering the activities of the Prime Minister for a period of four years, and not containing a single credential from this country, that he had not been in this country? We will have to accept the statement of the right hon. gentleman when he says he was a resident of Canada during all that time. I am merely pointing out that he leaves himself open to misinterpretation in that, as in other respects. He leaves himself open to further misinterpretation when he solicits testimonials and receives none from labour, whom he purports to have helped.
I have dealt with the reasons given by the Prime Minister as to why he could not support the amendment before the house.
We shall now turn to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), and find his position on the subject. The Minister of Labour addressed this house for three hours in an attempt to tell us that there was unemployment under previous Conservative governments; apart from that he said nothing. True, he made some sneering references to the Hon. Mr. 2419-84$
Ferguson, the premier of Ontario. I must say, however, that so far as his contribution to this debate is concerned, it has amounted to nothing. As has been pointed out in this house, however, he did say something in the city of London. His remarks are reported in the London Advertiser of Saturday, March 15, 1930. He is reported to have made a statement in regard to unemployment insurance. He has informed the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) that he stands behind the report as it appears in the London Advertiser, and I wish to direct again the attention of the minister to the report as it appears in that paper. I ask him if he did or did not make the statement as it is quoted? The first paragraph reads:
The Dominion government is ready to assist the provinces in establishing unemployment insurance for Canada on a contributing basis, announced the Hon. Peter Heenan, Minister of Labour in an address to an audience that filled Hyman hall last night. In making this important pronouncement Mr. Heenan said, "As far as I am concerned I will make every effort and the Prime Minister will back me up to see that the labouring man, who is out of work for any period of the year, will have a right to expect and to receive a share of the profits he helped to make.
Did the Minister of Labour make that statement as reported?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, I did.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. minister says he
did, and the result is that we reach a very unfortunate position for the Minister of Labour in view of the fact that the Prime Minister took a diametrically different stand. Later on in the speech of the Minister of Labour we find the word "assist." The Prime Minister has distinctly said in this house that he would not give a five cent piece to any Tory government. I interpret the remarks of the Prime Minister-and I hope I am not misinterpreting them-that he will not give one penny to any of the provinces, unless it is to one of the western provinces. In view of that fact, Mr. Speaker, we have one pronouncement from the Minister of Labour in London, Ontario, and another from the Prime Minister in this house. But worse than that, the Minister of Labour says he has the support of the Prime Minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I ask a question.
Are there not more ways of giving assistance than by making donations?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The only other way I know of is that the Prime Minister might give a copy of his book. I take the word "assist" to mean what it is commonly understood to
Unemployment-Mr. Ernst

mean, and as any audience of labouring men would interpret it, financial assistance. In the speech as reported here the Minister of Labour tells an audience of labouring men in effect that there would be financial assistance. What becomes of cabinet solidarity? We find the Minister of Labour making in the city of London a statement diametrically opposed to that made by the Prime Minister in this house. I will not use the word "misrepresent"; it is a nasty word and I believe it is unparliamentary but, sir, I will say the Minister of Labour deliberately misinterpreted the views of the government on the question for the purpose of getting a few votes in the city of London and elsewhere. Thus we have another illustration of this government forgetting one of the cardinal principles of responsible government, the principle of cabinet solidarity.
This is not the only illustration we have had; if it were the first perhaps it might not cause so much comment. We had the same thing happen with regard to the liquor export bill, with respect to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler). The same cardinal principle was forgotten, and we have the same situation all over Canada with regard to tariffs, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) when he made his address on this subject. For instance, we have our friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Crerar) who, I believe, purports to be an out and out free trader, and we have the Minister of National Revenue who campaigns Ontario as a protectionist. Down in my part of the country some gentlemen belonging to the party opposite are free traders, while some say they stand for "a tariff for revenue." I have not been able to understand what that means, unless it means to import as much as we can in order to get an increased revenue from the tariff. I have never heard a reasonable explanation of that term.
So we have the spectacle of one minister saying one thing in one place and another minister saying another thing in another place, with cardinal principles forgotten and vote-catching on every hand. How long can this country tolerate a spectacle of that kind under our Canadian institutions of government? How long can we have the Minister of Railways preaching free trade in the west while the Minister of National Revenue is a protectionist in Ontario? The result is exactly what you might expect, a species of tariff paralysis. The government cannot move in any direction, no matter how hard it tries; some one is always hanging on to its coat 
tails and pulling in the opposite direction. The government keeps moving simply in a circle, while the needs of industry are forgotten in the needs of political exigency. You get exactly the result you might expect to get. To-day industries here and there-I am not speaking of the farmers but of manufacturing plants-are idle; the Minister of the Interior can find plenty of cases in this province where men are out of employment because goods are being imported from foreign countries. Men are walking the streets and getting their bread from the municipalities, and the Prime Minister says the municipalities should feed them.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in the government of this country two things are essential; first, the principle of cabinet solidarity, and second, that a government which talks about its policies shall have some definite policy rather than the policy of helpless drifting.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been unemployment since time immemorial. The worst I remember was directly after the American civil war, when Ontario and Quebec were invaded by armies of men who were willing to do any kind of manual labour for their bed and board.
I was amused the other evening by the remarks of the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall). He flayed the Minister of Labour to the best of his ability, even accusing him of using bad grammar. While he spoke I thought that if his teachers and professors could have heard him they would have wept for his own inaccuracies and mistakes. The hon. member went on to claim that the Prime Minister was not what he should be, and so on. I want to tell my hon. friend that I happened to be in the United States during the last presidential election, and while I was there I heard some prominent people arguing about magazine interviews with the two candidates. While they were speaking I said, " How would your candidates compare with the Prime Minister of Canada?" For a few moments they stopped their argument, and both said, "We have no such men over here. We had to appeal to the gentleman who is now the Prime Minister of Canada to come to this country at a very strenuous period of its history." They referred to a time when capital and labour were at swords' points throughout the land, and the American government wanted a man who could cope with the situation. Princeton, Harvard and Yale universities were questioned, and each institution gave the name of Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. He went to that country and

Unemployment-Mr. Baldwin
saved hundreds of millions of dollars by starting industry working again; strikes were stopped almost entirely and capital and labour declared peace. That was a work worth while.
Then the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said there was an immediate need for this government to vote $500,000,	$1,000,000, $2,000,000 and finally
$3,000,000 for the relief of unemployment. Ever since I came into this house I have been in favour of making all criminals work for their living; I have opposed keeping people in prison in idleness. I would not give any money to ablebodied men who are able to eat their three meals a day. Surely we can find work for them to do somewhere. In the state of Vermont they are providing work in the beautifying of the sides of the highways, the removal of eyesores and obstacles and all that sort of thing. There is plenty of work in this country. I should like to ask the hon. member for South Wellington if he does not agree with me that to give money promiscuously throughout the country would be equal to the dole system in England, which has practically destroyed that country. I would not be guilty of doing such a thing as that. I am sure the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Black) and the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) would agree with me, if they were in their seats. The thrifty man Who has managed to accumulate some means does not desire to give his money to loafers.
Of course, I would not see a mother or a child suffer for food, but I say that ablebodied men in this country should not be fed at the expense of any government, unless they work. Certainly we can find work somewhere; we could build a trans-Canada highway across Canada, if necessary, but I never would vote for any measure which would grant money to idle able-bodied men. I believe, with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), that men loafing six weeks become hoboes, and men loafing six months in many cases become criminals. I believe that is altogether too true. I think laziness is a habit; after a time an idle person begins to hate work and will not support his family. Even criminals in prisons would work, if I had my way about it. They could do something; they could be taken on the land in the summer and help till the soil. It is a terrible thing to keep these criminals there in idleness, the young and old together, the criminal who has committed a minor offence herded in with the hardened criminal. That is a terrible state of affairs, and I would not allow it nor would I vote any money to be spent in supporting that class of people. There is enough
labour to be performed in this country. If the people who are without labour would work in conjunction with the municipalities and with the provinces, perhaps this thing could be worked out if the promise was given only to assist those rvho woidd work.
Who is to say that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways and other great corporations are not to get people from foreign countries? The presidents of those great railways have said for years that our railway and canal systems and the other great institutions of this country require at least a population of 15,000,000. When the United States was getting together its great population no immigration barriers were raised. People came to the United States from the utmost parts of the world. They came from many countries wh'ere the return with a thousand dollars would enable them to live in comfort for the remainder of their lives. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has great tracts of land which were granted to them before they built that railway, and they cannot sell it to Canadian people. Canadians do not want to work upon the land because their sons and daughters have been educated to enjoy the amusements and frivolities of the cities. They must have those amusements even although they have no money; they figure that they can commit some crime to put something into their own pockets, or get into somebody else's pockets. This country cannot be developed without that vigorous class of people from Scandinavia, Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Germany. We have some wonderful examples of what those people can do, and settlements can be found in the province of Ontario which demonstrates the thriftiness of that class of people.
Our people seem to have gone money crazy. Most of the girls in the country say openly that they will not marry anyone but a millionaire. If that state of mind continues, the birth rate will be controlled because that class of people do not want to be bothered with children.
The United States allowed people to enter that country without the least restriction. For many years on an average of 1,000,000 people annually arrived at Ellis island. Many of those people arrived in the early part of the year and returned home in the fall to remain ihere during the winter months. But that was possible because transportation by both land and sea was very cheap. People went on the land fifty, sixty and seventy years ago to obtain a living, but to-day their only thoughts seem to be as to how they can

Unemployment-Mr. Baldwin
enrich themselves. They become unhappy and troublesome and do not possess that love of country which would give them the desire to stay on the land and reap the return of an enhanced value. I have met people from the United States who settled on the land forty or fifty years ago and who are now able to rent their farms at such a price per acre as to provide them with world tours, from which they return once a year to collect their rents. They were a fine class of old country gentlemen, who lived quietly and biologically; they kept themselves free from disease and foolishness by sane life on the land. I am told that there are settlements in Ontario and in the northwest of people who have gone to those localities and who have stayed there. I do not know whether or not they built the so-called dug-outs, or whether or not they built pole houses with thatched roofs, but they became thrifty, they own their land and have money with which to buy additional acres. That is the class of people we must get to populate this wonderful and magnificent country. Our boys and girls will not consider a life which requires so much labour and which deprives them of the amusements and frivolities of city life. They want to have automobiles and spend their time running and gadding about the country.
This may not be the time to mention this subject, but I was told by an aviator in Montreal-by the way, I believe in aviation, although I do not care to go up myself at the present time-that out of twenty-eight accidents which occurred last year in Canada, twenty-seven were caused by the man at the controls. I will not mention this terrible accident here in Ottawa, outside of saying that my friend knew that aviator very well. It will be necessary to enact more stringent laws than we have to-day, governing the licensing of air pilots. If we had enough Lindberghs in this country there would be very few accidents, and if I remember rightly, Lindbergh was a Scandinavian. I think his mother came over from Norway or Sweden, and she is now teaching in the state of Michigan. They said Lindbergh was crazy, but he did not prove to be so crazy when he left America to cross that boundless and ice-covered territory for Europe. If Lindbergh were in this city to-day, and had the time I would not hesitate one moment to go up in the air with him. Tests should be made of those men who are to guide these ships of the air. They should live according to all biological rules, and not be excessive in anything. They should not partake of any stimulants, and should be clean livers. But, Mr. Speaker, I

do not suppose that these remarks would apply to the relief of unemployment.
Unemployment is caused largely by the great increase in inventions. Many newly invented machines are doing the work of several people, but there is one class of people who come from the old country, for which there is a great need-domestic servants. In the eastern townships there is a continual waiting list for this class of immigrant, and it is almost impossible to obtain a domestic who will remain a domestic for any great time.
Men cannot be found who do not insist on employment for the full year. Generally Speaking, the farmer can employ only one man and woman for the entire year, although he may need additional help during the summer season. In olden times there were plenty of unmarried men who would remain with the farmer or the lumber man during the slack season for a nominal amount plus his board. But there is no more of that; they say: "If I cannot get the big pay I got when you needed me, I will not work for the small pay when you have not much for me to do." Domestic service is one of the best employments in this country for an uneducated girl, because she gets her board and generally she has as good a room as any member of the family; in fact, she is usually regarded as one of the family. If she is getting $5 or S6 a week, she does, not realize that her room may be worth 85 or $6 a week and surely her board is worth as much. If she were to go to a city for employment and secured a job at S15 a week, she would hardly be getting as much as she does as a domestic. But she thinks she does not have as much liberty as the girl in the city. Perhaps not, but by staying on as a domestic and learning what a wife's duties should be she has a much better chance to become a healthy girl and a good wife and mother.
To come back to the unemployment question, it seems to me so silly-because, as I said at the beginning, unemployment has been with us from time immemorial-to raise all this hue and cry and berate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan). The hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) made against our esteemed minister bitter charges which were very different from what the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) had to say about the minister. I do not believe any hon. member in his heart of hearts would defame the Minister of Labour; nor do I think in their right minds they would make against the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) accusation not befitting at least a young member

Unemployment-Mr. Baldwin
As regards this contention over matters that cannot be controlled there is but one remedy, and that is for the government to carry on public works and to give a fair remuneration to the people employed on them. These works are diversified in character; there are wharves, rip-rapping to keep the rivers in their proper channels, public buildings and highways. I cannot believe it would be a good policy for the government to construct national highways, although the United States are giving vast sums to the different states, and they call the roads so assisted government or state roads. We have in this country many places that can be beautified and made productive by the expenditure of money, let it come whence it may. In this way we could give work to our people who wish to work, and if we have in Canada foreigners who do not want to work, I would have them deported. The period within which they can be deported is five years and we have in this country some vicious men who should have been deported before that period elapsed. About every week when I am in Montreal I see quite a number of people who have just come to Canada, and I am glad to see them come if they will help to develop our wealth; because we heard it said during and after the war that we needed people to develop our naitural resources and to help to pay our national debt. Surely if we can get people who will cost the country nothing to bring them here, it is a good idea. Everyone is pretty well agreed that assisted immigration should stop, and I believe no more money should be spent in that effort. Everyone knows that Australia is not very alluring at the present time. There were a few years when Australia was attracting more people, but she is at present in a bad financial position; England does not seem to be getting much better, while Germany and some other countries are getting worse. I do not say that we want a Mussolini to rule in this country, but in Italy the chief ruler makes the people stay on the land.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is a fact. Mussolini does not allow people Who are living on a farm to leave it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In this country many
people want to remain on the land and they are not allowed to remain there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Has the mortgage been
foreclosed?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A man who would do
that is hardhearted. I have many mortgages,
but I have never yet intimated to a man that he should get off the land. I would rather give a man a farm than foreclose him, because the courts are all in sympathy with the man you are foreclosing and you would not foreclose many men before you would get sick of your job.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Probably in the hon.
member's province the farmers are not obliged to pay 8 per cent interest on farm mortgages.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A good many years ago,
in all the border states as you went across the Mississippi right out to the Pacific coast, the ruling rate of interest was from 10 to 12 per cent. It is not many years since you could lend money in Oregon at 8 per cent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is what has driven thousands off the land in the United States.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is characteristic in
newer sections that are not so well established. The west is a long way off, thousands of miles. The wealthy people in New England lent their money in the middle western states, for instance, Wisconsin, Nebraska, Minnesota, and the Dakotas, and many banks were ruined. When a bank was ruined there was no hope of getting the money back; but if a person lent money out there and saw it was no use to dispossess the farmer but that it was better to hold the land, pay the taxes and wait for better times, he was all right, because the value of land doubled, trebled and quadrupled and the eastern investor who was not avaricious got his money back years later. It is characteristic of America at least that interest has been high to the people on the western frontier, right to the Pacific coast. But I am sorry to learn that in this age of community spirit, with only ten banks now throughout Canada, our people in the west have to pay more than 7 per cent. Seven per cent is the ruling rate of interest throughout the east except to people who can command large sums of money, and of course such people can hypothecate gilt-edged securities and secure money for 6 per cent. Thirteen years ago, when I came to the house, I remember statements being made that the rate of interest was 10 and sometimes 12 per cent, so that conditions have been alleviated to some extent if the rate has been reduced to 8 per cent. I believe, however, that rate will be reduced before very long. The grafters, gamblers and brokers in the United States the year before the collapse of the stock market were getting practically all the money in that country and paying 7 and 8 per cent for it, while legitimate business went begging or even went into

Unemployment-Mr. Baldwin
bankruptcy on account of not being able to secure money. Now, with money at 3 or 4 per cent in New York, the situation is different and I suppose interest rates will become easier.
As regards immigration-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Tell us about unemployment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: For sixty years the situation has been just the same as it is in 1930. And here we are with a beautiful April shower this morning to release the frost from old mother earth and start her blossoming in all her glory. Is there any reason why people should hang around the cities unemployed? I would vote for a law to make an able-bodied man work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What if he wants to
work and cannot get it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Those are world conditions, my dear man, and you and I cannot do anything about them. I have trouble in getting help to work for me. I have been here two months and my son has written me several letters in that time saying that he cannot get help to start the mill. As a matter of fact, there are more people looking for work and praying that they won't find it than my hon. friend imagines. There are people who want to live and die in laziness. The farmers of this country are working fifteen and sixteen hours a day. Those are my hours, but I would work only nine or ten hours a day if I could get help to relieve me in my store and in my mill and in the woods. Conditions are such that people will not stay in the rural sections of the country. Some woman wants to get out and show her finery, and she does not care how she gets it, by hook or crook.
I am glad the chain stores are developing in this country. The old-time merchants who sell goods on credit now have to compete with the Atlantic and Pacific, the Stop and Shop, the Dominion Stores, and all the other chain stores. It is going to be a good thing for the country. We merchants have lost hundreds of thousands of dollars trusting goods to everybody that wanted them. Some would claim to be sick for six months and would be getting goods on credit, and then when you finally refused any more credit, I have had one say, "I have not been sick a day this winter." He did not tell me that; he was afraid to, but he would send some member of his family. Finally when spring came I would tell such people: It is time for you to get out and shift for yourself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Tell us about unemployment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am telling you some of the conditions I meet with. I have already spoken about servant girls. I have had two or three from England, and- I assisted them over. The last one had high ambitions. She wanted to be a nurse. She thought Canada was the size of England, and that the little Baldwin mills must be right close to Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver, that she could jump in a trolley car and reach them in no time. Naturally she was disappointed. My wife told me that she was a lady of attainments. I lent her sixty dollars to go to Vancouver, and she repaid me every cent. Another one, without attainments, wrote me from Windsor saying that she could not get into the United States and would be deported. She wrote me for twenty-five dollars, and I replied; "If you had stayed at my place, you would have had $150 in the savings bank and would not need to borrow."

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Did she get the twenty
five dollars?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Most emphatically she
did not. The Lord helps those who help themselves. I do not put myself on a par with the Almighty, but I like to see people do something for themselves. My hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) asks me how I would deal with unemployment. I will tell him:	Get to work. You cannot put
any energy into sissified, pussyfooting and spineless people. If you knock them down, they might get up and come at you. There is no other way under the sun. You can lead a horse to water but you cannot make him drink, and so long as men can stay around the city and town and sponge their living, many of them will not work. There are several ways of begging. There is the polite way of living on your friends, borrowing money from them. That is simply giving your money away because they do not intend to pay you back. The sum of $337,000 has gone out of my office here in the last six years and I never expect to see a red cent back, but my philanthropy is a little less now than it was then. I have learned a considerable amount about human nature, and the man you help most is the one who will evade you, who will not speak well of you, and at election day probably will be the last man to vote for you.
There is no way in which we can sit here and legislate to make people work. Legislation will not stop unemployment. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) wants $2,000,000 or $3,000,000 taken out of

Unemployment-Mr. Esling
the treasury to relieve unemployment. I would not let a woman or child go hungry in this country, and there are hundreds of thousands of other people who feel just the same way, but I would not vote to help an ablebodied loafer. I would make him work if there was any law in this country to make him do it. I know from my own experience that it is easier to do your own work than to get any of that class to do it for you. I think our Minister of Labour is doing all that any minister of labour could do. I notice that my thrifty friend from Halifax (Mr. Black) and my hon. friend from Lincoln, who I understand have accumulated a good deal of this world's goods, are not jumping to their feet and saying: Grab the money out of the treasury to relieve this awful unemployment situation. I have not heard a word from them, not one, and I do not think we shall hear from them in this debate. Are we never going to think of the people in this country who toil and labour and delve, working overtime? If they have accumulated money by their own hard work, are we going to tax it out of them to the last cent? There were too many in the last war who stayed at home and said: We will spend the last dollar. They had a flippant tongue, but no capital, and were mighty glad not to go to the front. I know that class, even ministers of the gospel. It is not laughable.
AVhen we talk about alleviating unemployment, there are old rookeries in Montreal and other cities that we could get rid of and put up public buildings there. I do not want to repeat what has been said about not giving a five cent piece to a Tory government, but I will say this, that if the Tories were in power they would not give a five cent piece to a Liberal government. I was never a very bigoted politician, and I believe there are good people and bad in every party. It may be suggested that one way of relieving unemployment would be to tear down our old, unwholesome buildings and embellish the sites with new and beautiful structures. But then the government would have to go into the rental business, and people who moved in woidd say: This is government property and we should live here free. There are a lot of people too lazy to work who think they are quite capable of running the country. I do not suppose there is a member here who is not asked by some of his constituents now and again: What are you doing up there in Ottawa? And then they proceed to tell him how parliament should be conducted. Whole multitudes think they should get into the civil service and have soft jobs because a few
Toms, Dicks and Harrys under the old patronage system got into the service, although they were as illiterate as jack rabbits.
It takes money to alleviate unemployment.
I believe a trans-Canada road would be a good investment, if it could be undertaken. It should be built as far north as possible, say, up by the Hudson Bay railway, so you would hold tourists from across the line the maximum time. Up there they would find it cool and breezy. But I would not allow them to bring in more than a thousand cigars and ten thousand cigarettes. I have known some pretty smart customs officers who thought tourists should not bring in a carload of cigarettes and cigars, but these officers were found fault with because-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because of climatic conditions it would be both unreasonable and unjust to charge the government with responsibility for all unemployment in Canada at this time: but where such unemployment is caused directly or indirectly by reason of government policy or lack of policy, then it seems to me that the government should accept responsibility. It is only in connection with the bearing that government policy has on unemployment that I should like to add a few words to this debate.
I regret very much that the Minister of Health (Mr. King) has absented himself from the house, because he is the minister from British Columbia representing East Kootenay, and I simply make this reference in passing for the reason that throughout the province of British Columbia to-day there is no district in which unemployment conditions are more deplorably distressing than in the district which the minister represents. Up until a few weeks ago the coal 'mines in Fernie were getting out about sixty carloads of coal daily; then conditions changed and the production was curtailed to the extent that fully one half of the coal miners are out of employment to-day and the other half are working only part time. I have before me the Nelson news, the daily paper in that district, which gives details of the actual conditions under the heading:
Fernie miners' children hungry-three hundred miners unemployed following mine shut down-all credit stopped.
Conditions there were so bad that the various communities were called upon to endorse a resolution which was sent to the government. It was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and also to the minister from British Columbia (Mr. King, Koot-

Unemployment-Mr. Esling
enay), and I can assure them that those worried wage earners and the distressed mothers and hungry children cannot be satisfied by the usual reply the government give, that "they will take the matter under consideration." The matter became so critical that the miners and people of Fernie called a mass meeting at which they passed the following resolution:
Whereas we have reasons to believe that the Crowsnest Pass Coal Company is controlled by American capital, and whereas we have reasons to believe that at a recent meeting of President Hoover and the chief industrialists of the United States, the slogan of "Buy U.S.A. products" was adopted, and whereas through the adoption of such a slogan the Great Northern Railway cancelled all orders for coal with the Crowsnest Pass Coal Company causing three hundred men to be laid off by the said coal company,
Therefore be it resolved that we the Fernie miners now assembled request the federal government to investigate the now distressing conditions prevailing in the mining district of Fernie,
Be it further resolved the Fernie miners request the federal government to assist in sending in immediate relief and thus relieving the distress now prevailing amongst the miners of the Fernie district.
No. (2), that we request the federal government to stop all immigration until all residents of Canada be employed permanently.
No. (3), that we ask that the moneys now being used for immigration be utilized as a subsidy for freighting coal from Alberta and southeastern British Columbia and so find employment for unemployed miners in this district.
It is interesting to look back to see just how the present conditions were anticipated some years ago. I find that in 1925 the right hon. Arthur Meighen introduced the following resolution :
That to enable the products of the western and maritime provinces to reach more readily the markets, the special transportation burdens borne by these provinces should be shared by the Dominion, either by contribution to long haul freight costs, or by assistance in some other form.
Strange to say the minister from British Columbia, who represents federal policies in that province, voted against the resolution. It will be interesting to see what explanation he will make when he reaches Fernie in a few days. No doubt he is on the way there for the purpose of fixing up his political fences, but he will have so many questions to answer in relation to his stand on matters which are close to the hearts of the people of British Columbia, that I really think it will be rather embarrassing for him.
I want also to put on Hansard a resolution passed at a meeting of the Sandon miners' union last January:

Whereas; The present immigration policy of the Canadian government has a detrimental effect upon the Canadian workers, and,
Whereas; All cities in Canada are burdened with unemployment and a large number of them are forced to establish relief work and soup kitchens: we, the members of Sandon Miners' Union, in meeting assembled, contend that no nation can survive on soup kitchens, thus lowering our standard of living, and,
Whereas; The prairie provinces have stated definitely their opposition to assisted immigration, and steamship or railway subsidized immigration, as they have now a surplus of unemployed. Therefore, be it
Resolved; That we demand that all immigration to Canada be immediately discontinued, and that the government take immediate steps to establish unemployment insurance, and be it further
Resolved; That copies of this resolution be forwarded to the Premier of Canada, the Ministers of Immigration and Labour, Jas. S. Woodsworth, M.P.. W. K. Esling, M.P., and the Hon. J. H. King.
They, too, recognize the fact that the immigration policy of this government is contributing to unemployment, and it will be seen they ask that immigration be restricted and the policy of unemployment insurance established by the government. I repeat that I regret the minister is not here to state his attitude in connection with these problems.
At this time I shall refer to another matter which is directly connected with government policy, namely, the position of the man on the land. I refer to the man who purchased land, cleared it, planted his crops and hoped to receive some return from his investment and labour. On three different occasions the Minister of Health voted in favour of permitting the entry into Canada of surplus farm products. The strange thing is that the minister seemed to blow hot and cold1; when he went- through British Columbia he talked one way, and in the House of Commons he voted another way. His statements to the people of West Kootenay and East Kootenay are not borne out by his vote in this house. Having voted to permit the influx of these surplus farm products, he went into the Okanagan district and said that the Dominion government was fully alive to the situation created by the lack of anti-glut duty on vegetables. It seems incredible that any minister of the government could hope to ride two horses at once, but we find that to be the policy of the minister from British Columbia.
There is another question of policy arising out of the matter of highways. There is no doubt in the world that the construction of highways would have absorbed much of the present unemployment. To my mind there is nothing which the people of British Columbia

Unemployment-Mr. Esling
would welcome more than highway construction, and there is no doubt that it should result in the construction of a trans-Canada highway. In the year 1919, the government contributed $20,000,000 for that purpose, and the resolution of the hon. member for Atha-baska (Mr. Kellner) merely asked for a continuation of that grant, so that the provinces could carry on the work. Surely such a building program would have materially relieved the present unemployment situation, and opposition to such contributions must necessarily be the policy of every Liberal candidate in the coming election. The minister from British Columbia voted against any aid to highways.
Hon. members in this house will no doubt remember the resolution of the member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy). He asked for the immediate construction of a Pacific coast outlet from the Peace River district. He did not stipulate a specific route, but asked that the best possible route should be taken. He did not tie the government down to anything in particular, but merely advocated construction by the best possible route. In this connection we find the minister from British Columbia going into the city of Vancouver and other cities along the coast, and telling the people how enthusiastic he was about the Pacific coast outlet, when only two or three months previously he had gone on record in this house as being opposed to it.
I wish to make some remarks about the Doukhobors. I do not touch upon this subject for the purpose of amusement, because we have had enough amusement in connection with this very serious situation. The position of the matter is serious, particularly in its relation to unemployment. The Doukhobor settlements are fast growing communities. In those districts we find two or three Canadian citizens who may have put all they owned into a piece of ground ten or twenty acres in extent; they have planted an orchard and have made a living. The Doukhobors have come in and bought the property of one of the settlers, with the result that the other two move away. Canadians will not live alongside of these people; they do not want to, and nobody wants them to, I told you before of an instance where a whole Doukhobor family was working nude in the field, and the wife of the neighbouring farmer was compelled to submit to the embarrassment caused by such conduct. These people are not only making it impossible for the Canadian farmers, vegetable growers and others to compete with them, but they are entering other fields of industry. I may tell you that the late Minister of Immigration and Colonization, Mr. Forke, sent to British Columbia and received a special report on Doukhobor activities. In that report there is information as to how men were being driven off the land because the Doukhobors had no hours of work, no wages to consider, and their products were turned over in competition with those of the local farmers. To-day we find the Doukhobors are an important factor in the pole and tie industry. In 1928 there were 31,000,000 feet of poles cut in British Columbia. Of that total 21,000,000 feet were shipped, and much of this was controlled by the Doukhobors. Surely when we realize that these people have entered into the different fields of industry in competition with Canadian labour, we appreciate the fact that we have another reason for unemployment. I wish to refer to the policy of the government in regard to these people, and to point out that although they were admitted to this country as far back as 1898 and bonused to come here, they were excluded by the Conservative government in 1912. Things progressed very well until 1926, when the minister from British Columbia, conscious of the competition which existed, joined the government in passing an order in council throwing down the bars and inviting more Doukhobors to come in. I shall be keenly interested to learn how he will explain this matter when he goes before his constituents. This is a policy which each Liberal candidate in the Dominion of Canada must accept when he enters the coming election. We find the minister from British Columbia absolutely out of step with all the policies in the immediate interests of the people in his constituency.
In regard to these matters I want to fortify my contention by specifying certain matters in respect of which the minister's attitude is on record in Hansard, so that there can be no controversy about it. In the first place we find the minister on record as being opposed to grants for the Pacific coast outlet from the Peace River district. We find him opposed to technical education. He has placed himself on record on three different occasions as being in favour of the importation of surplus farm products at glut prices, and he is also on record as being opposed to giving the returned men the benefit of the doubt in their applications for pension, in cases where disability has occurred after discharge. We find him on three further occasions opposed to the abolition of the sales tax on boots, shoes and clothing; these are commodities which the unemployed must buy. He is on record as being opposed to federal aid for the construction of highways, and he is in opposition
1332	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
also to any contribution in connection with long haul freight costs on western products. Western products are products of British Columbia, and products of the coal mines at Fernie; and he is therefore on record as being in opposition to any contribution to long haul freight costs on Fernie coal. There is another paragraph in the resolution which places him on record as being opposed to any other kind of assistance in the marketing of Fernie coal, so I am sure the minister will have a very pleasant time fixing up his political fences when he reaches home again.
I have referred to these questions purely as matters of policy affecting unemployment. There is no doubt that the minister, together with every other Liberal candidate at the next election, will have a hard time explaining just what are the policies of this government, and why he supports so many government measures which are contrary to the interests and welfare of the people of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I come to my remarks, which will be rather short, I should like to refer to some of the points brought up by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton). It seems to me he did not attempt to deal with that part of unemployment which affects the municipalities and which has become a burden to them. He mentioned seasonal unemployment with regard to fishermen and ' sailors. I come from a constituency in which there are very many of these two classes of people, and I find that we have very little trouble with them. They are employed in the summer; they count the summer as their year of employment, and they are no burden and no menace to the municipalities.
Then the minister suggested that the municipalities might take upon themselves the construction of sewers and work of that kind during the winter. I might remind the minister that this already has been done by almost every municipality in Ontario. He also referred to the fact that building operations might be extended into the winter, but the men who are engaged in the construction of buildings do not enter into the question of unemployment. From the statistics issued by the department here at Ottawa it will be seen that the list of unemployed does not contain any union men so that the references of the minister to the fishermen and the sailors, the construction of sewers and the extension of building operations do not really go to the point at all.
This amendment has occasioned quite a lengthy discussion, which indicates that the subject is a live one in many parts of this

great Dominion; that it is not only a matter of local interest but that it has a wider aspect. The hon. member who moved the amendment evidently had this wider aspect in mind when he moved his amendment, but those hon. members who have spoken for the government have put the question on a very low plane. The speech of the Minister of Labour indicated that this was merely a question of party politics, but as we all know that is not the case.
Reference has been made to the calling of a conference to discuss this matter, and it was thought that such a conference, if called, would have done a great deal towards the solution of the problem of unemployment. However, the government refused to call such a conference, and nothing has been done. So far as I can see, nothing but good would result from such a meeting; you cannot enter into discussion of this great question without taking many interests into consideration, and surely the calling together of men representing different interests all over the Dominion would bring about at least a sincere consideration of the question. However the government has chosen to disregard that suggestion and has ignored the wider aspect of this grave question.
I know the Minister of Labour has a really warm heart and would turn from his way to help the poor, hungry people of this country, but in the provincial legislature, where I knew him very well, as well as in this parliament, evidently he fell in with very poor company. At all events, he has been unable to influence this government It may be that he had the wrong password in approaching the mercy seat; he may have taken the great book Industry and Humanity with him; but I am afraid that book has been given the wrong title-it should be called Industry and Party Politics.
The Prime Minister has refused the amendment, and I think during the course of his speech he made the greatest slip of his political career. Prime Ministers always have been looked upon rather as the fathers of the people, persons to whom suffering men and women can come and relate their miseries. However, our Prime Minister of to-day has lost that human touch; the working man of Canada now must assume his party toga, put on his party stripe and approach the throne if he wants a job. This has been the case in Ottawa; working men have paid their dollar fee, secured a badge and card, and then have been sent down to the party leaders to see about it. Even now that Liberal working man in Ontario is forgotten by the

Unemployment-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
Prime Minister, who says he will not give one five-cent piece to any Tory government for unemployment. The Prime Minister must mean by that, if he means anything, that the Liberal working man of Ontario must go to Prince Edward Island or to Quebec if he wishes to receive any aid from the federal government. The Prime Minister has hoisted his flag and sounded his slogan, which is "Vote Liberal or starve".
In answer to the Prime Minister, however, who has laid this great burden first upon the municipalities and then upon the provinces, and who has been seeking out funk-hole after funk-hole in which to shelter himself, I would say that funk-holing will not relieve him of his great responsibility in connection with this matter. There are very strong associations relating this question to the federal government. The Department of Trade and Commerce has been referred to; the making of treaties, with their consequent effect upon the people of this country, has been brought up also, and I shall not discuss it further. The fiscal policy of the government has affected unemployment. I would like to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to this fact; in my constituency at least two industries have been forced to cease operations because of the fiscal policy of this government. What is the position of a man who has been put out of work because of this fiscal policy? First, he may become idle; second, he can move over and take the other man's job; or, third, he may migrate. Whatever course is followed, unemployment is produced by an act of this government. The great textile industry has been affected, and one plant in my constituency which filled a great need in providing mixed employment has closed its doors. These employees have the choice of idleness, taking the other man's job, or migrating.
The effect of immigration upon unemployment has been mentioned, and I do not intend to discuss that phase any further. Unemployment lies at the root of practically every social problem in this or any other country, and the present government cannot escape responsibility. Crime increases during the days of unemployment, and such crime always affects to a great extent the life of the community. I do not think that any citizen of our land would not prefer to have a full dinner pail rather than free government rations in a penitentiary, jail or prison.
The great number of unemployed are not affected by the excuse offered by the government that much is being done for the returned man. The returned man claims as his right that which has been done for him, and that
fact cannot be offered as an excuse to the unemployed. The government having refused to discuss or consider the wider aspects of this question of unemployment as brought out by the amendment, we are driven to this course; the only thing remaining for us to do is to bring to the attention of the government some local matters which are affecting unemployment in our different constituencies. Although I do not agree entirely with the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton), he has said that seasonal unemployment affects every constituency where the labouring man is to be found. There is much that the government could do to relieve this situation. It is quite true that the railway companies have been urged to continue construction work, and that the manufacturers of locomotives and cars have been asked to keep their plants running, but the government should go a step farther and see that the work is continued throughout the winter time. Contracts have been given in my own city which could just as easily have been started in December as in February.
It has been claimed that the government is rendering assistance through the large construction works being carried on. In most cases of this kind a large mass of labour is moved from some unknown point into the locality where the work is under construction, to the disadvantage and to the ousting of local labour. That situation applies to every large construction work carried on by the government. The government should see that local labour receives the benefit or its share of such work.
This government has given contracts for the construction outside of this country of many necessities which could be manufactured within the country. I take my stand with the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Thompson), who mentioned the building of ships. When the claim was made that these ships could have been constructed in Canada, the only reply given by the Minister of the Interior was, "Oh, nonsense." Does the hon. minister believe that the Canadian workman has an inferiority complex, and thinks that this work cannot be done in Canada?

speechtext:
The only reply we received was, Oh, nonsense. We were told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it would cost 40 per cent more, but if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) were to use the same method as practised in giving coal contracts, this difficulty could be overcome. I have before me a return brought down this year which shows
1334	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
that tenders were called for coal supplies. The friend of the government was not the lowest tenderer, and what did they do? He was given two successive chances to bring his tender down below the lowest tenderer. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce would adopt that method, many articles at present manufactured outside of the country could be built in Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce must know of the investment in shipyard equipment, and he should realize that something should be done for this industry. Over $100,000,000 is invested in this industry; we have dry docks, and we are extending others to accommodate larger ships, but if ships required for Canada are not built in Canada, what chance has that industry to develop? Is this $100,000,000 to be thrown away, and are the efforts made to build up this industry to be ignored?
Surely the government can give some further consideration to this industry, which in turn affects a great many other industries. Our steel mills, the carpentry trade, our railroads, are interlocked; in fact, I do not think there is any industry which affects so many other industries as does that of shipbuilding. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce would only give our shipyards a chance to repair Canadian ships he would be doing something. Year after year, I have brought to the attention of this government the difference between the attitude taken by the United States on this question and the attitude taken by Canada. When an American ship comes to a Canadian port to undergo repairs, she is taxed 50 per cent of the cost of the repairs when she returns to her home country, but Canada does not make the same provision. If the directorates of our steamship companies were placed on the same plane as they are in the United States, then we would have more ships built in Canada and more repair work would be carried on in our dry docks.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Before six o'clock
I had pointed out that the amendment implied a consideration of the wider view of unemployment; that the suggestion of a conference was merely an attempt to crystallize the Canadian view; that it would gather together people with many varied interests and would be followed by beneficial results, and without any injury, even though it failed to 
effect a complete cure. The government, however, refused to consider the wider aspects of this subject and chose to discuss it from the lower plane of party politics; and perhaps the lowest plane was reached by the Prime Minister when he avowed-not once; but repeated that he would not give five cents to any Tory government for unemployment. The slogan, therefore, in the next election will no doubt be: Vote Liberal or starve. It has remained, therefore, for us to point out where unemployment could be reduced by government action, and before six o'clock I had been discussing shipbuilding and repairs to shipping in this province.
I had pointed out how the United States protected her shipbuilding and ship repairing. Perhaps I can best indicate in a few words the interest they take in the matter of providing employment for their people in this work by saying that under the United States law no ships may engage in coastwise trade unless they are built, owned and documented in the United States of America; while, for many years, the Canadian fleet has not been a credit to Canada or to our national industry. Secondly, on repairs to American vessels made in Canadian yards the United States collects fifty per cent duty at the first port of call. Canada's rates on repairs to Canadian vessels in American yards is twenty-five per cent only, and that is payable only if and when the vessel reenters Canadian coastwise trade within a year. The house will readily see, therefore, that American vessels will take care to have all their repairs done in American repair yards, and that very little of it will come to Canadian yards. But if the government are alive to the interests of Canadian workingmen they can see to it that these repair yards of ours, as they are on the inland lakes at least, get their fair share of repair work. That would affect beneficially several constituencies in this province. As I said at the beginning, the government having refused to consider the wider aspects of this question of unemployment, we must come down to these local conditions, drawing them to the government's attention and requesting the government to take an interest in the protection of Canadian workingmen.
Closely allied with that subject has been the government's refusal to assist in technical education. With ship repair yards in this country actively engaged, we can provide employment for a great many of our workingmen; but with technical education I think we can do very much better. I look upon unemployment, as has been pointed out so many times in this debate, as a fluctuation.

Unemployment-Mr. Coote
Men in this country are drawing away from what you would call pick and shovel work to employment demanding more in the way of technical education; we have a very large field for their technical skill, and as a result a small field for those without technical training. That condition could be corrected by taking care to give the boys who are growing up to the age of manhood a technical education that would at least lead them into the fields of technical work and fit them for those skilled occupations for which there is a greater demand in this country.
I am not going to take further time. I have drawn the attention of the government to these conditions which are, I confess, local to my own constituency, and pointed out how the government could provide employment for many men. I would ask the government seriously to consider that technical education has a great deal to do with unemployment in this country, and I think that any federal government would be well repaid for any expenditure that it made for this purpose. The government would be well repaid to look at this thing from a humane standpoint. I know that there are a good many warmhearted men amongst the ministers; I know that our friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) if he were only free from the company he is with, would look at this question from the humane side, instead of supporting the laying out of great parks and public squares and the beautifying of capitals, not only in this country, but elsewhere. If the government would only look behind all this beauty and see the frantic condition of the unemployed father and mother, and the pitiful condition of the hungry children and emaciated boys and girls, if they would only consider the plight of the boys and girls handicapped by the want of food and care, I feel that I should not appeal to them in vain. We want a big, strong, healthy population, and we have the country and the stock to produce it, but if this unemployment situation continues, if the government lets our boys and girls go hungry and obliges them to stay away from school for want of clothing, then there will be produced a condition in this country that it will take a lifetime to bring back to normal. Above all, when we bear in mind the vital issues at stake, we should not be concerned whether this is a municipal, a provincial or a federal matter; we should view it from the standpoint of the future of Canada, and deal with it in the interests of our boys and girls, the coming men and women of this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many other members, personally I am very tired of this debate, and were it not for the fact that there is a great deal of unemployment in my own constituency, I would not take up the time of the house by speaking to-night. I am sure most of us are rather sympathetic with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who is anxious to get the house into committee of supply. But in my constituency there are a large number of unemployed men, particularly in the coal mining area. When I was there last December I found most of the men were working only one day in the week and occasionally two days. There are five large mines in the district, and I think that statement generally would apply to them all. I find on inquiry from the bureau of statistics that last year -1929-the HiMcrest Collieries worked 192 days; the International Coal and Coke Company mine at Coleman worked 190 days; the McGillivray Creek Coal and Coke Company mine worked 210 days; the West Canadian Collieries Greenhill mine worked 176 days, and at Bellevue 173 days. This means that if a miner worked every day the mine was open at Bellevue he would get 173 days' work in the year. That man must be on hand ready to answer the call of the mine whistle every workday in the year if he wishes to get in that 173 days' work. Taking all the mines together they averaged only 188 working days in each mine.
This is a very important industry. The output of this district,-and it is practically confined to these five mines-in 1928 was 1,639,000 tons. Bearing in mind what I have just said, that one of these mines worked 173 days in the year, I should like to give to the house some figures as to the wages these miners earned. I am quoting from an article entitled Mining Conditions in Alberta, which appeared in The Canadian Unionist of February, 1930. It is written by Frank Wheatley, Vice-President of the All-Canadian Congress of Labour and President of the Mine Workers' Union of Canada. He says:
Contract miners earn as much as eight to ten dollars per day, and as little as $5.40 per day in the organized sections of the coalfield. In the unorganized sections wages are often as low as $2.50 per day, and these low rates are as inimical to the interests of the coal-owners as a whole as they are to the welfare of the miners who receive them. The day-wage scale runs from $4.20 for outside labourers to $5.50 for skilled workers, such as carpenters, mechanics, etc. Labourers inside the mine are paid $4.45; horse drivers, $4.90 to $5.25; miners, timber-men and track-layers, $5.40 to $5.57.

Unemployment

Mr. Coote
Any miner who worked 173 days at $4.20 per day would earn a total of $726.60 in the whole year. The highest paid labourer outside the mines is paid $5.50 a day, and if he worked 173 days he would earn $951.50. This man must hold himself in readiness to work any weekday in the whole year to earn this amount. Most of these men have families to keep. Personally I do not think anyone in this house would say that any of these miners could possibly keep his family for a year on that amount.
I have here a letter from the Secretary of the Mine Workers' Union of Canada at Coleman, dated January 14, 1930, so this is comparatively recent information as to the situation there. He says:
The International mine is working on an average of two days per week, and there are around 200 men employed.
I may add that when that mine is working at full capacity in the summer time it employs from 400 to 500 men. He continues:
The McGillivray mine is working with 250 men. The miners' union has spent about $1,800 on relief.
That is, the miners' union at Coleman.
The companies have not donated a cent in cash, but through our efforts we got about 25 married men at the International mine and 13 married men at the McGillivray mine temporary work.
I am only quoting briefly from this letter as I do not wish to take up too much time. The writer goes on to say:
There is no indication that work has or will improve in the near future and although we have obtained temporary relief for the majority of married men at the present moment we have still a serious state of affairs confronting us. There are between 60 and 70 single men in the camp who have done no work since July and we cannot get the authorities to do anything for them. The union has reached its limit in this direction and what is to become of them is a problem. The majority of them are immigrants brought to this country under the present immigration policy supposedly for another class of labour, but drifted into the mining camps thus creating the present situation.
That is one of the grounds on which I wish to bring the attention of the federal government to the situation existing there. The problem is due largely to our immigration policy or lack of policy. I want again to emphasize one point in this letter. The writer says:
There are between 60 and 70 single men in the camp who have done no work since July.
That is six months. You might wonder how these men have lived. Let me relate the

experience of an immigrant that I met in Coleman. He came to Canada in 1928, taking advantage of a harvester excursion from England. He worked in railway construction gangs for a few weeks in the fall of 1928 and was finally sent to Coleman by the employment office at Calgary. When he interviewed the gentleman whose name had been given to him by the employment officer, he said he did not want any men for three weeks. This man and two others who went with him stayed at Coleman for three months before they secured any work at all, and during that time they were boarded by a Chinaman who runs a boarding house there. These men said to me, frankly, they did not know how they could have existed if it had not been for the bigheartedness of the Chinaman in furnishing them with board and meal tickets for the three months before they got work.
I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in outlining the policy of the government towards the question of unemployment relief said that the first duty of providing such relief must fall on the municipalities. I want to show the government how impossible it is for a municipality like Coleman to take care of the unemployed that are there at the present day. In this town seventy per cent of the taxes are levied on the homes of the miners themselves. Now, if the miners are working on the average only 188 days in the year at wages such as I have quoted, how is it possible for that town to take care of the local unemployment situation? It may be possible for the larger municipalities to take care of a problem such as this, but it is not possible for small municipalities, such as those in these mining districts. In this case, the municipality, I believe, have spent $1,000 in relief work. They gave work for the purpose of assisting these men who were in need of relief. Yet that thousand dollars is only a drop in the bucket to what was really required. The miners themselves have suggested a remedy for the situation as it there exists. I may say that over 90 per cent of the coal produced in this bituminous coal district is taken by the railway companies; in this particular case I think it is practically all taken by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The railway companies take the bulk of their coal during the months of April, May, June and July; sometimes they begin taking it out in the month of March. Because of an immigration policy under which a large number of the miners have come from the old country under the guise of agricultural labourers, the mining companies have been able to put on as many workers as they wished. They work

the mines to full capacity, and are able to fiill the orders of the railway company in four or five months of the year; for the remaining six or seven months the work slackens diown to one or two days a week. The suggestion of the miners is that if a conference were arranged between the operators of the mines and the railway company, the railway company might be persuaded to spread their orders over a longer term of months. The miners' union passed a resolution last November dealing with this matter, and I think I shall take a few minutes to read it so that it may be recorded on Hansard. It is as follows:
Whereas the period of time worked by the coal miners of the Crowsnest Pass mining district of Alberta is yearly becoming less though each year a larger tonnage of coal is produced;
And whereas it has been the practice of the coal mining companies to employ many hundreds of transient miners for a few months of the year to meet the orders for storage coal required by the Canadian Pacific Railway from that district, with the result that those workmen engaged in the mining industry permanently are not able to obtain sufficient work during the balance of the year to secure a living for themselves and their families causing the expenditures of much money by the provincial government, municipal councils, and the trade unions for relief purposes;
Therefore be it resolved that repesentations be made to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on whose railway system 90 per cent of the coal productions from the said mining district is used, asking this company to so regulate their orders for coal that the productions may be spread over a longer period of the year, thus enabling those persons permanently required to man the industry throughout the year to obtain a livelihood without further having to seek relief from various sources; and, failing satisfactory adjustment along the lines suggested, that the federal and provincial governments be requested to institute a measure of control within the industry through the appointment of a body similar to the present railway commission under whose direction such mismanagement shall be corrected.
This matter has been brought to the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan). I first brought it to his attention last year and received his hearty cooperation. It might fairly be said that due to his efforts the situation at the present time is better than it wold have been had he not intervened. At this time I wish to ask the Minister of Labour to go a little farther and to try to arrange such a conference as has been suggested. I think that the operators and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should both be represented at this conference, and it is my opinion that the federal government might take the initiative in arranging it. The men who are keeping up these towns and keeping up their schools are what might be called the 2419-85
Unemployment-Mr. Coote
permanent employees of these mining companies. I think in all fairness the work should be confined largely to them, and it could be done without any great inconvenience to the railway company. I ask the Minister of Labour to urge upon this government the necessity for initiating such a conference. May I point out to the Minister of Labour the seriousness of the situation at the present time? Because of the small crop which had to be handled last year I understand that this year the railway companies are asking tenders for half a million tons less coal than they took in 1929, and if no action such as is suggested is taken we will have more unemployment than we had last year.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) asked this afternoon for some concrete suggestions. It is my intention to accede to his request, and to put some suggestions before the government. The operators of the bituminous coal mines in Alberta and eastern British Columbia have estimated that 465,000 tons.of American bituminous coal are consumed annually in the province of Manitoba; this figure does not include the coal consumed by the railway companies. I am informed that the Canadian Pacific Railway is using Canadian coal as far east as Kenora, and I make that statement because someone said yesterday that American coal was being used as far as Moose Jaw.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They do not, as far as I know; all that coal is going to the railways. I do not think any of this coal is going east of Winnipeg except what is used by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The operators in Alberta are paying a very heavy freight rate on their product to Winnipeg. The rate from Bellevue to Winnipeg is $5.10 per ton. That is a distance of 841 miles. The cost from Fernie to Winnipeg is $5.30 per ton.
I should like to repeat something I said a moment ago: This year the Canadian Pacific coal requirements will be something over half a million tons less than they were a year ago, and certainly that will cut down employment a good deal. Just here I might quote one sentence from a letter which I received from one of the operators recently. He said:
You will readily understand that the subvention is absolutely necessary if we are even going to approximate last year's working time and if that fails, there is going to be more distress among the workers than ever.
I should like to mention also, Mr. Speaker, that I have received numerous telegrams and letters from the different locals of the miners' union in that area, all asking that this subvention be granted. I believe the secretary of the operators' association wrote to the minister suggesting that this arrangement might be made for a period of three years, which would give the operators time to prove that their coal is just as good as some of the American coal which finds so much favour in the Winnipeg market. The word "Pocahontas" when used in connection with bituminous coal,

seems to be like the word "Keen's" when applied to mustard; we know there are other good brands of coal on the market, but if a person can say "this is Pocahontas coal" it seems to sell right away. I believe that if this subvention could be granted for a period of three years Canadian bituminous coal would establish itself in Winnipeg.
Some objection may be taken to this proposal because of the cost it will entail, and I recognize the fact that this matter should be carefully considered on that account. However, I should like to direct attention to the fact that up to the year 1924 the government received $1,051,000 in royalties from the mines I have mentioned. I do not know what these royalties would amount to since that year, but from rentals, royalties and the sale of certain coal lands, the government received from the companies in that district practically $1,500,000 up to the year 1924. I am sorry my figures are not up to date.
Then I have one other suggestion to make in regard to the coal industry. I think it will be generally admitted that in no other industry in Canada, taking it over a long period of years, has there been so much unemployment on the average as there has been in the coal industry. I am going to suggest to the government, in addition to the two suggestions I have made already, that they appoint a royal commission to investigate this coal industry. This was done in Great Britain some years ago, and I think it is largely as a result of that action that the present government in the old country have introduced some very drastic changes affecting the coal industry there. The appointment of this commission has been requested by the All Canadian Congress of Labour and also by the Mine Workers' Union of Canada.
