I have both resolutions here; the one passed by the All Canadian Congress of Labour reads as follows:
Whereas for a decade the Canadian coal mining industry has been subjected to such abnormal depression as to reduce the mining community to extreme poverty, due largely to the lack of coordination of supply and demand, with waste of labour power and natural resources; be it
Resolved that this congress call upon the government to appoint a royal commission to investigate conditions in the industry and to find a remedy.
I wish to quote briefly from an editorial which appeared in the Canadian Unionist, with regard to this proposal. The editorial states:
A careful inquiry by a royal commission might therefore point the way to such improvements in organization as would not only raise the mine worker from the coolie status but also add immeasurably to the wealth of the country.

Unemployment-Mr. Johnstone
The state of the coal mining industry has recently been given close study by the government of Great Britain, and reorganization of both production and distribution has been decided on, with restraint of wasteful competition, as the most practicable immediate reform. On a smaller scale, the industry in Canada is in much the same condition as in Great Britain, and it is believed that an official inquiry, by a royal commission, would be the most effective means af ascertaining the cause of the present distress among the miners and of evolving a remedy.
Now I wish to quote the resolution passed by the Mine Workers' Union of Canada, which is as follows:
We request that a royal commission be appointed immediately with a view to stabilizing the coal industry as a whole, by investigating the living conditions, sanitation, discrimination against outside purchasing of goods and necessities, "closed" or "company owned" towns, cost of living in the coal camps as compared with the cities, marketing and distribution of coal, etc., all with a view of alleviating the present distress and poverty among the miners and their families in Alberta and eastern British Columbia.
Before I close, Mr. Speaker, I want to assure you that there is real distress among many of our miners. Recently I received a letter which told of the conditions in one town, where the miners were so poor they were not able to pay for their milk. The milkman notified the mounted police that he was not going to deliver milk to a large number of these families any longer, as he said he must have money for his milk in order to pay for the feed he gave his dairy cows. One cannot blame the milkman, but if the miners are in such dire circumstances that they cannot afford to purchase milk for their children, I think this government might very well appoint a royal commission to examine thoroughly into the coal industry and make such recommendation as they may see fit for the improvement of the status of the people engaged in that industry. I think the responsibility in this case is primarily on the Dominion rather than on the provincial government, because as I see the situation in Alberta the trouble has been caused largely through the unfortunate results of our immigration policy. The majority of the men who consider themselves capable miners are immigrants, and I think a majority of these immigrants came to this country under the guise of agricultural labourers. I think there is no question at all but that the present situation has been brought about largely as a result of our immigration policy. Therefore I do not feel that I should make any apology whatever for asking the Dominion government to
take the responsibility of dealing with this whole question of relief to the unemployed miners, rather than to ask the province to assume that responsibility.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. W. JOHNSTONE (Cape Breton North-Victoria):
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to
say a few words with regard to the amendment now before the house. This is a very important matter which seriously affects my constituency, which is largely made up of miners and labourers.
Several theories have been advanced in the hope of solving this unemployment problem. A few days ago, in looking over some literature, I came across a theory which I thought might be applicable to my constituency, and perhaps to some others throughout the country. It was called1 the theory of underconsumption, or the failure of consumption, to keep up with the swelling current of production. The writer thought this was the best solution of this unemployment problem, and certainly it has to dlo with conditions which exist in my own constituency,
Some two months ago a conference Was held between the operators and the miners over a question of wages, and after a great deal of deliberation they decided upon a contract. A referendum was taken a few days ago and the contract was upheld by quite a large majority, so that to-day the people of Nova Scotia have a contract rate which will continue for two years. But where is the employment to come from to provide those wages? We could produce more coal in Cape Breton if we had a market. Last summer our principal pit was working with but a single shift, and this year our mines have been working only one day and a half per week, simply because we did not have markets for the coal we could produce. I feel that I am perfectly justified in placing the blame for this state of affairs upon the fiscal policy of the Dominion government.
In 1929 we imported into Canada 4,019,917 tons of anthracite coal, and 13,707,543 tons of bituminous coal. When such a flood of coal is imported into a coal producing country like Canada, is it any wonder that the operators, and also the men dependent upon their industry for work, are discouraged? That importation represents $2,000,000 in wages, and it means less employment for our Canadian workmen. But the government is doing absolutely nothing to relieve this situation' or to prevent the enormous inflow of coal, and therefore I think I have a perfect right to put the blame upon the government fiscal policy.

Unemployment-Mr. Johnstone
Had the government fully implemented the report of the Duncan commission, considerable assistance would have been given to the maritime provinces. For many years we in the maritime provinces have been trying to have coke ovens erected throughout the country, and have tried to educate the Canadian people in the use of coke instead of hard coal. A bill to that effect was presented in this house, but nothing ever came of it. How can we expect to do anything when coke is allowed to enter this country free of duty, as well as American coal to be used in the manufacture of coke. Can we expect any help from a government which permits such conditions to exist?
I believe that if this government would offer assistance to the provinces it would be accepted. My own province has enacted the Women's Allowance Act, which allows 860 to $70 per month to any woman who is unable to work and support her children. If the Dominion government would take the lead in this matter, it would assist the provinces very materially, but after hearing the remarks made a few days ago by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the effect that he would not vote five cents to a Tory government, I do not see where there is much chance <of our receiving any assistance towards tha relief of unemployment. However, Mr. Speaker, there is always a bright side to everything. The bright side to this question .3 the knowledge that within a very short time we will have a government that will see that justice is done to the provinces of tha Dominion irrespective of their political faith.
Unemployment would be reduced through the use of our own raw materials, instead of their being sent out to the United States. Why not manufacture the finished article with our own material and use the labour of our own people? Some hon. member has said that the United States, which is a high protection country, has a great deal of unemployment. I can well understand why that is true, because a great number of those unemployed are Canadians who left their homes to look for work in other countries. The United States has taken a stand in this matter. The city of Detroit, where there are a great number of Canadians, has taken a definite stand on the subject. There are many people in that city from Cape Breton, and I have many letters telling of the inability to obtain work, in many cases the writers not having the fare to come back again. Many nurses in the hospitals of Detroit have been dismissed, although I

have heard since that some have been reinstated on account of their efficiency. The United States cannot be blamed for taking this stand. They say: "We cannot give you foreigners any work, we must protect our own people. Surely j'ou have a government in Canada and you can obtain work there. Go back to your government and ask them to give you work; do not come to us." The United States government are protecting theii people, and our government should protect our people.
Some hon. member has mentioned the displacement of the workman by the machine. Scientific inventions are found to-day in practically every industrial centre. It would be hard to find to-day an old fashioned handpick miner in our mining districts. The only solution of this problem is more factories and industrial centres. We should build up our highways, and carry on other construction work, so that our men could obtain emploj'-ment. Whatever solution is offered for this problem, the government of the day must take the lead, whether it be b>r the appointment of a commission or the creation of industries to provide work. The majoriy of our workingmen want work; they do not want charity. How can we do this? It could be done by the development of the great resources in which Canada abounds. Perhaps we will always have more or less unemployment, but if this condition can be relieved to any extent it is our duty to offer that relief. The hidden wealth of this great country of ours should be brought to light to provide work for our workingmen. They want work but they are unable to obtain it. It seems strange that this government cannot afford a certain amount of employment to our own people so that they need not go to foreign countries in search of employment. If that were done, then we could say in perfect truth that we are not able to say to-day-Canada for Canadians.
Mr. ROBERT K. SMITH (Cumberland): Mr. Speaker, I am in absolute accord with both the spirit and the letter of the amendment moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I believe the government should not only take immediate action to deal with the question of unemployment at present existing in certain sections of Canada, but strive to work out some formula to anticipate the grave question of unemployment which it and all succeeding governments will encounter in this country from time to time. As the hon. member for North Winnipeg very properly said, it is always our most

Unemployment-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
vital question. I had no doubt that in respect to this matter the government would trot out and hide behind the British North America Act, as it usually does, and which it did on this occasion; nevertheless, the problem of unemployment is still to be solved.
I am a firm believer in protecting the working classes in this country. This seems to me to be one of the greatest national questions we have to deal with. Like all matters of social legislation, it is important, far-reaching and expensive, and I believe the attempt to shoulder these heavy responsibilities on the provinces is unjust and grossly unfair. Take, for instance, the question of old age pensions. All heartily agree with the principle of old age pensions and are anxious to have the legislation enacting it implemented in the nine provinces of Canada. But how can that be fairly adjusted in a provincial way when the cost to one province is as high as 35 per cent of its total revenue, the cost to another only 10 per cent, and the cost to other provinces, I understand, in western Canada, as low as 2 per cent? The house may think what it likes, but it is quite apparent that this is the happy day of advanced social legislation for our working classes. That being admittedly the case, some of the smaller provinces are not financially capable of keeping pace with this very worthy legislation to assist our working people.
Old age pensions and unemployment are questions that must be dealt with sooner or later if we are to have a happy and contented country. In my opinion-and I am giving my own opinion-the only way in which they can be effectively dealt with is nationally. The government will say: Why, if you saddle us with aid to highways, aid to technical education, public health and matters pertaining to social legislation, you will exhaust our treasury. My answer to that is that under the British North America Act the federal authority is vested with all the elastic sources of revenue and can so regulate its revenues to meet any financial exigencies. The provinces cannot do that. In the final accounting a tax removed from a province and imposed by the federal authority works no injustice to any taxpayer. The burden is none the heavier, and I am of opinion that the only effective and successful way of giving the working classes in Canada a real chance to enjoy the privileges and advantages of modern social legislation is to place those matters of which I have spoken under federal control and authority.
It seems to me that altogether too much stress is laid upon the division of the burden
of taxation as between the federal and provincial- authorities in hewing so close to the line of technical interpretation of the British North America Act. If a citizen of a province who is also a citizen of the Dominion is relieved of a provincial tax and that burden is absorbed by the federal government, no injustice is worked. The citizen does not pay any more, but it certainly would have the effect of standardizing, harmonizing and equalizing civilization and advancement in all the provinces, which, after all, make up the Dominion.
We have under the present allotment of jurisdiction under the British North America Act between the federal and provincial authorities, two very unfortunate sets of circumstances: first, the (financial inequalities of the provinces; secondly, the more financially fortunate of the provinces being able to provide legislative relief of a social character to their citizens, which relief is denied in other provinces. This creates a state of unfairness and inequality that is unhealthy and the very antithesis of what I understand to be a united and contented Canada. Could anything be more anomalous than to find in one province the citizens enjoying, say old age pensions, unemployment insurance, mother's allowance, minimum wage laws, eight-hour day and other rights, and in another province of the same Canada, the same confederacy, the same union, the citizens enjoying none of these benefits? That state of affairs can be tolerated only so long, just long enough to break both the spirit and the letter of confederation.
Questions of a national character must of necessity be dealt with by the federal authorities and I consider the question of unemployment fundamentally and primarily one of national import. In this connection my mind goes back to the treaty of peace signed at Versailles on June 28, 1.919, where the following will be found as part of that great document. I am quoting part XIII of the treaty, section 1, which reads:
Whereas the League of Nations has for its object the establishment of universal peace, and such a peace can be established only if it is based upon social justice;
And whereas conditions of labour exist involving such injustice, hardship and privation to large numbers of people as to produce unrest so great that the peace and harmony of the world are imperilled; and an improvement of those conditions is urgently required; as. for example, by the regulation of the hours of work, including the establishment of a maximum working day and week, the regulation of the labour supply-
1342	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
And, mark you, Mr. Speaker,
[DOT]-the prevention of unemployment, the provision of an adequate living wage, the protection of the worker against sickness, disease and injury arising out of his employment, the protection of children, young persons and women, provision for old age and injury, protection of the interests of workers when employed in countries other than their own, recognition of the principle of freedom of association, the organization of vocational and technical education and other measures;
Whereas also the failure of any nation to adopt humane conditions of labour is an obstacle in the way of other nations which desire to improve the conditions in their own countries.
Following that, article 387 of the treaty sets up a permanent organization for the promotion of the objects set forth above, and in the annex to chapter IV of article 424, it specifies the place of the first meeting as Washington and it supplies for that meeting the agenda which includes among other things the application of the principle of the eight-hour day or the forty-eight hour week, the question of preventing or providing against unemployment. It goes on to mention many other matters of social legislation of importance in this connection. Section 2 of article 427, under "General Principles of the Treaty of Peace", reads as follows:
The high contracting parties, recognizing that the^ well-being, physical, moral and intellectual, of industrial wage earners is of supreme international importance, have framed, in order to further this great end, the permanent machinery provided for in section 1 and associated with that of the League of Nations.
They recognize that differences of climate, habits and customs of economic opportunity and industrial tradition, make strict uniformity in the conditions of labour difficult of immediate attainment. But, holding as they do, that labour should not be regarded merely as an article of commerce, they think that there are methods and principles for regulating labour conditions which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply, so far as their special circumstances will permit.
Among these methods and principles, the following seem to the high contracting parties to be of special and urgent importance.
Then it goes on to enunciate nine such principles, most of which were enumerated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the speech that he delivered the other day. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, would any sane person contend for one minute that these important and worthy matters of social legislation are not national in character? Furthermore, the provinces as such were not signatories to the treaty of Versailles. The federal authority had that grave duty to perform, and having gone that far should continue responsibility and make some effort to conform to their sacred pronouncements and their national obligations.
(Mr. R. K. Smith.]
Back in 1922 I had the privilege of appearing before a Senate committee on unemployment, and I was greatly impressed with the evidence of one of the representatives of labour whose name I have for the moment forgotten. He said in part that while the war was in progress and recruits were being sought, solemn pledges were freely given that when the war was over and victory had been won, there would be a general reconstruction and reestablishment of people and conditions in this country. What class, he asked, needed reconstruction and reestablishment? Certainly not the wealthy. It was meant for one class and one classe alone, the one that needed it -the working class. Perhaps if there had been a measure at least of conscription of wealth as well as of men during the war, we would be in a better position to attain that ideal to-day.
I believe, in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come when this vital problem so seriously affecting our working classes should be treated in a spirit of national consciousness and righteousness, from a broad and uniform viewpoint, and with the fact always staring us in the face that our commitments are clear and great, our obligations unfulfilled, and as a consequence our national honour at stake.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In
rising to support the amendment of my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), I believe that the question of unemployment is one in which every hon. member of this house should be particularly interested. I believe that the people of this country are anxious that a solution of this problem should be found. They realize that the greatest asset of any nation is its citizenship, that the men who carry the dinner pail, the working men, are those who are largely responsible for producing the wealth of any country, and that a government that does not provide a policy that will enable these working men to be gainfully employed is not measuring up to its full responsibility.
I entirely agree with the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) in his statement this afternoon that in a country such as Canada we are bound to have a certain amount of seasonal unemployment. I cannot agree with him, however, when he states that the men who are employed during the season of navigation are found among the ranks of the unemployed when navigation is closed, and that they are seeking assistance during the winter months. It is true that many of them are unemployed during the

Unemployment-Mr. Simpson
winter months, but we find very few of them seeking assistance, because they figure that the wages which they receive during the season of navigation will be quite ample to take care of them during the winter months.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They are fresh water
sailors anyway.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes. That we have an
abnormal unemployment situation at the present time has been admitted, I think, by practically every hon. gentleman who has participated in this discussion, with the exception of the Minister of the Interior and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). We have had speaking in this debate representatives from the west and from as far east as Sydney, Cape Breton, and we have heard them describe the conditions of unemployment in their particular localities. Some of them cited cases of extreme hardship. Yet we find that the ministers who have spoken have offered no real solution for this unemployment problem.
What is the resolution before the house? It simply asks that immediate action be taken by the government to deal with the question of unemployment. A broad resolution, a resolution one would imagine that should be accepted unanimously by this house; but we find the Prime Minister devoting the greater portion of his speech to an endeavour to prove that we are enjoying great prosperity in the Dominion of Canada and that there is no abnormal unemployment situation. We have the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), more familiar with the labour situation because of the position that he occupies as head of that department, admitting that we have more than the ordinary amount of unemployment, but offering no solution. Both of them, as well as the Minister of the Interior, are going to vote against this amendment if it comes to a vote, thus shelving the question for the time being, washing their hands of all responsibility and passing the responsibility over to the municipalities and the provinces.
There can be no doubt that the municipalities and the provinces have some responsibility in connection with unemployment, but in my judgment, Mr. Speaker, the federal government also has responsibility in connection with the unemployment situation as we find it to-day. If under a policy of immigration such as this government has maintained, immigrants are brought into this country and find their way into various municipalities without those municipalities asking for them, and where there is no work for them to do, will anyone contend that it is the responsibility of those municipalities either to find work for those immigrants or to care for them until such time as work can be found for them? That surely is a responsibility that should rest upon the government that admitted those immigrants to this country.
My hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) in the course of his excellent speech stated that in one of the western provinces at least sixty-one per cent of those who were receiving relief were immigrants. The Manitoba Free Press, in an editorial, states that of the number registering for assistance in the city of Vancouver, seventy per cent are immigrants. Surely the federal government have some responsibility to those who have come in as immigrants and are to-day a public charge.
I am opposed to the present system of immigration. I do not believe this country should spend, as it has been spending during the last several years, an average of over $3,000,000 annually for the purpose of bringing in immigrants, when at the same time our own citizens have been leaving the country by the tens of thousands, following our raw material over to the United States in order to secure employment in fabricating it into the finished product, much of which is shipped back into this country. What we need is a policy to provide more jobs for our own people. Once that is done there will be no difficulty about immigration. Once we have more jobs than w'e have Canadians to fill them, you will find desirable immigrants rapping at your door asking for admission. Then you will not need to spend any money on advertisements such as those my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Hay) read to the house this afternoon.
Might I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government is responsible for unemployment from another aspect? The fiscal policy of this government, their policy of tinkering with the tariff, has been responsible for a certain amount of the unemployment that we are suffering from at the present time. Take, for example, agricultural implements and automobiles. The trade treaties that this government have negotiated and their downward revisions of the tariff have made it easier for the products of other countries to come in here and compete with the products of Canadian labour. Let me draw the attention of the house to the effect of the policy of the government in reducing the duty on agricultural implements, which they provided for in the budget of 1924. Immediately after the budget had been presented to the house a deputation composed of manufacturers of agricultural

Unemployment-Mr. Simpson
implements-including our present ambassador in Washington, Mr. Massey-appeared before the government and pleaded for some relief, stating that the proposed reduction of duties would ruin their industry. They succeeded in getting relief, the government making provision for the free entry of all the steel that goes into the manufacture of agricultural implements, and for a drawback of duty on many other commodities entering into their manufacture. What was the result? An increase in the import of agricultural implements from the United States in the fiscal year of 1929 over 1925 of about $33,722,000; the imports for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1925 being $6,428,549 and for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929, $40,150,020. Who got the benefit? The workmen in the United States, because the farmers in this country did not reap any benefit as a result of the reduction in the duty on agricultural implements. My hon. friend from London (Mr. White) in a speech he delivered in the session of 1928-the very year for which these figures are given, the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929-quoted the prices of agricultural implements from the price lists of the International Harvester Company, which showed conclusively that notwithstanding the reduction in the duty no benefit had accrued to our farmers by way of a reduction in the price of their implements. Then let us take the reduction of the duty on automobiles in 1926. When the reduction was announced in the budget our automobile manufacturers appeared before the government and stated that the reduction would ruin their industry. The government treated them just as they had treated the agricultural implement manufacturers-gave them a drawback of the duty on some of their raw materials, and the remainder of it admitted free of duty. Ihis reduction of duty produced a similar effect, the increase in our imports for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929, over the fiscal year ending March 31, 1927, amounting to $41,314,000; or a total increase in the imports of these two items alone of $75,036,000.
Figuring on the basis laid down by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) last session, when he stated that for every dollar of value of the manufactured article fifty cents represented labour, and taking an average wage of SI ,500 a year, these additional purchases from the United States would have provided employment in this country for 25,000 workmen, and those workmen could comfortably support a city of
125,000	population. And it must be borne in mind, Mr. Speaker, that I have taken into account only the raw material that entered into the manufacture of these agricultural 
implements and automobiles. Their raw material is the finished product of other manufacturers in this country, for instance, the finished product of the primary steel manufacturer. I could cite the conditions obtaining in that industry at the present time, but I refrain from doing so.
I submit, sir, that having regard to the figures that I have given the policy of this government has a direct bearing on the unemployment situation as we find it to-day and therefore we might very reasonably expect the government to accept the amendment as proposed by my hon. friend from North Winnipeg; but they are passing the responsibility on to the provinces. A question of this nature should be treated on its merits, it should be above partisanship, but we find the Minister of Labour trying to blame the premier of Ontario for not proceeding more rapidly with highway construction, claiming that that would have provided against a certain amount of unemployment; but the Minister of Labour himself voted with the Prime Minister against the resolution that was moved in this house to grant federal assistance to the construction of highways, particularly the completion of the trans-Canada highway. I think everyone will admit that if that work had been proceeded with it would certainly have provided employment for a considerable number of men.
I must say I was amazed at the statement the Prime Minister made in this house the other day. He said that so far as the government was concerned with respect to this question of unemployment it would not give a five cent piece to any province where there was a Tory government. Was there ever an exhibition of more extreme partisanship than that indicated by the statement of the right hon. gentleman? Instead of treating this great humanitarian question on its merits he tells the people of five provinces of this Dominion that because in the exercise of their citizenship in a free country they decided to elect Conservative governments, they cannot expect from this government a five cent piece for the relief of unemployment. I suppose that is the reason the government turned down the proposals for assistance in the construction of highways and1 for technical education. The people of Canada have the right to expect something better than that from their Prime Minister. I submit that this government, by reason of its immigration and fiscal policies, is largely responsible for the unemployment problem as it exists to-day; for that reason they should accept this amendment and assume their full responsibility as a government to deal with this question.

Unemployment-Mr. Quinn

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not intend to take up much of the time of this house in speaking to the amendment of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), but I feel it incumbent upon me to say something in regard to it, and to make a few humble suggestions to the house as to what I consider would remedy or alleviate the unemployment situation in Canada.
The hon. member for Cape Breton North-Victoria (Mr. Johnstone) referred to the steel and coal industry of Nova Scotia. May I point out to the house that four years-ago, in 1926, the Duncan commission made its report to parliament, and in that report it recommended that the steel and coal industries should receive the favourable consideration of this government. After four years of waiting the^ government has failed to implement the recommendations contained in the Duncan report with regard to these two very important industries. I can tell the house that the steel workers of Canada, particularly in the province of Nova Scotia, are becoming restless, and as a proof of that statement I am going to -read to you an article not from the Tory press but from the Ottawa Citizen of Friday, April 4, 1930. It is a Canadian Press despatch and is as follows:
A resolution urging that adequate tariff protection be afforded the steel industry in order to give employment to citizens of Canada, reduce privation and alleviate the unemployment situation which is singularly acute, has been forwarded to Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Premier of Canada, and members of his cabinet by the general works committee of the employees representation plan, representing over three thousand steel workers employed by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company.
I ask you, sir, if that is not worthy of the consideration of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heen-an), of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and of this government? We have heard a resolution from the workers praying that the government do something to alleviate the unemployment -situation in this country. On Friday last the member for East Simcoe (Mr. Thompson) pointed out that ships for the Canadian government to be used in Canadian trade and industry might well be built in Canada. During the course of the hon. gentleman's remarks he was interrupted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), but in a gentlemanly fashion. The minister on that occasion pointed out that it would cost nearly 40 per cent more to build these ships in Canadian shipyards. May I say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is my friend, and I admire him in many ways; on that occasion he was making a statement in favour of protection, and I am told) the
minister is a protectionist. He pointed out that it would cost 40 per cent more, and in my opinion he made an argument for a 40 per cent tariff on foreign built ships. If we pay a higher rate for ships built in Canada, where does the difference in cost arise? The materials are purchased in our own country, the ship from the keel up is built of materials produced in our own country, and the building of the ship gives employment to vast numbers of workmen in the steel and iron trades, the different metal industries, the furnishing industry, the electrical industry and all other industries which contribute their proportion towards the building of a ship. Do not forget that the most important thing of all is that you are giving employment to thousands of Canadian workmen, and instead of sending your money abroad you are keeping it at home. By the building of those ships in Canada we are buying our own materials from our own citizens, and are giving employment to our native workmen. I ask, sir, if that is not one of the best arguments with respect to the amendment now before the house. I may say that I pointed out this fact to the government during the debate in this house on June 10 of -last year, and at that time I advocated that Canadian ships required for the Canadian government and its different departments should be built in Canadian shipyards.
A couple of months after my return to Halifax the International Association of Machinists on August 2-2, 1929, passed a resolution in the following words:
We wish to call your attention to the matter of steel shipbuilding in Canada. You will readily understand that the federal government is responsible for furnishing transportation facilities for our commerce, both on land and water. It has been the policy of all Dominion governments to subsidize our railways, both by grants of lands and moneys. They have been very successful in inducing companies to erect plants to construct locomotives and passenger cars of the largest types built anywhere, and at the present time we have two of the largest railway systems in the world, which are able to get all their rolling stock built in Canada.
Now we wish to get your assistance in inducing the Dominion government to have all ships, whether passenger or freight, that are used by the railway systems and government departments, built in Canada. The Canadian Pacific Railway system has had a number of ships built in Great Britain at a cost of over $50,000,000. The Canadian National Steamships, a government concern, had five ships built at a cost of $8,000,000, and have given contracts for three more ships to cost $5,000,000, all of which are to be built in Great Britain.
This means that over $63,000,000 of Canadian moneys have been sent across to Great Britain to build ships, when, if these ships had been

Unemployment-Mr. Quinn
built in Canada, it would mean that the amount of money would have been put into the pockets of shipyard workers of Canada.
It is easy to see the reason for this policy of having ships built in Great Britain. The standard of living is higher in Canada, because the Canadian worker demands and receives higher wages. A comparison of Canadian and United States methods in having ships built is suggested. The United States government, in placing contracts for the carrying of United States mail stipulates that they must be carried on ships built in the United States, and they have cooperated with the steamship companies in placing orders for ships in the United States shipyards. Some of the steamship companies have paid over twice as much for ships to be built in United States shipyards rather than send their orders to Great Britain or Germany.
If the Americans can do that, why cannot the Canadian government and Canadian companies do that which tends to keep the money in circulation in Canada? Therefore be it resolved that we adopt the following resolution:
Whereas, during the Great War the building of steel ships was found to be possible in Canada, and taking into consideration the immense resources of this country, the development of which is reaching enormous proportions;
Be it further resolved, that the trades and labour organizations use every effort to bring pressure to bear upon the government to take the necessary steps to encourage the steel shipbuilding industry in Canada.
That is a union, sir, in my own city of Halifax. They are not wrong in their views and they are not sectional in their outlook either. I should like to point out that similar resolutions have been adopted by unions in Quebec and Ontario. I have another resolution here, which is dated at Halifax, March 15, of the present year:
Felix P. Quinn, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
I have been instructed by Halifax Lodge No. 765, International Association of Machinists, to forward to you the following resolution.
Whereas the increased business activity of the maritime provinces especially between the mainland and Prince Edward Island calls for greater transportation facilities on the Canadian National railway and demands the building of a car ferry to be equipped with facilities for the transportation of automobiles which the present car ferry does not possess.
And whereas there are shipbuilding firms with yards equipped for building ships such as the car ferry required in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, it is for this reason that Halifax Lodge No. 765, International Association of Machinists wish to place themselves on record as protesting against the placing of the contract to build the car ferry to any firm of shipbuilders outside the maritime provinces.
Respectfully yours,
E. J. Rudge,
Recording Secretary Lodge No. 765, International Association of Machinists.
In the discussion of a few days ago the question of the Prince Edward oar ferry was
IMr. Quinn.}
dealt with by the Minister of Labour, who told us that that contract had been awarded to a firm in Quebec at a very much higher figure than the government would have had to pay in Great Britain or some other European country. I oan quite appreciate that statement; I know how true it is and I must congratulate the minister, if he had anything to do with having that contract placed in a Canadian shipyard. I regret very much, however, that since the steamer was to ply between two of the maritime ports, the contract was not placed with the Halifax shipyards, because I understand that the difference in the contract price was only some 15,000 or $6,000. Having regard to that fact, I hope the contract price will be adhered to. I hope we will not have a situation similar to that which arose a few days ago, when we were dealing with the estimates for the province of Quebec having to do with harbours and rivers. There was an item of some $27,000 for some firm in Quebec, and when the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) was asked for an explanation of the item he told the committee it was because that amount of loss had been sustained by the firm under a contract with the government. If after the ship is completed this shipbuilding company comes to the house with a request for a grant from the government to cover a loss sustained under that contract, if I am here I will bring the matter to the attention of every hon. member. That would be unfair competition; if firms are allowed to tender and contract with this government at an unreasonably low figure, in the hope of coming back to parliament and asking for a subsequent grant to make up the loss, I contend that it is a very poor principle and a very unbusinesslike way for the government to deal with such matters.
With regard to the resolution passed by the Halifax branch of the machinists' union, I may point out that under date of February 22 a memorandum on the need of tariff protection for the shipbuilding industry of Canada, addressed to the federal government and members of parliament by Gaspard Langlois, president of the Shipworkers' Union of Lauzon, Quebec, along similar lines, appeared in the Montreal Gazette. Towards the end of the article I find the following:
The shipbuilding industry of Canada is going through a very serious crisis, says Mr. Langlois. Former prosperous yards have hardly sufficient work to justify their maintenance. And while Canadian shipyards are nearly silent, Canadian companies are constantly awarding shipbuilding contracts to other countries.
I point this out to the government for their consideration, and ask them whether the unemployment situation would not have been

Unemployment-Mr. Lapierre
greatly alleviated if these contracts for Canadian ships had been placed with Canadian shipyards. The article continues:
Nearly $100,000,000, it is said, has been invested in the effort to reestablish shipbuilding in Canada: most of it has been sunk, apparently. Of course, the effort to revive Canadian shipbuilding involved considerable investment in subsidiary industries, which, also is all at sea.
The hope of the Lauzon workers that the "Canadian shipbuilder will be given protection equal to that enjoyed by his neighbour the American shipbuilder" is not, unfortunately, likely to be realized while the present government is in powder, anyway.
I must admit that I share the views of that gentleman.
I listened to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) telling the house that in his opinion the tariff would not remedy the situation, and he made the statement that high tariff countries were not without their unemployment problems. Let me point out to him the difference between England and France. England is a low tariff country, and has nearly 2,000,000 people unemployed at the present time. Contrast that situation with France which is a high tariff country, and which has only 1,500 unemployed. France is a country with five times the population of Canada but with only 1,500 unemployed, of which about 1,200 are in the city of Paris. I give those figures on the best authority; I have taken them from the latest issue of the Commercial Intelligence Journal, which is issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce under the administration of the Hon. James Mal-solm. On page 512 is an article by Hercule Barre, the Canadian trade commissioner, dealing with the commercial and financial situation in France. He says:
According to official figures on February 18, the number of unemployed in France totalled 1,521, of which 1,134 were in the Paris district.
If a protectionist tariff is so beneficial for France, then this government should consider whether a similar protectionist tariff would not be favourable for this country and tend toward the relief of unemployment in the Dominion of Canada.
The hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) the other day pointed out that the trend in the west was toward protection. I believe that the trend in the whole of Canada is toward protection. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) showed me a report which stated that the Liberal candidate for that constituency had declared that he was for protection, and that the Liberal candidate for the constituency of Vancouver-Burrard also had declared himself a protectionist and had denounced the new
tariff amendments of the United States. The workingmen of Canada want protection for the industries which give them employment, but I am afraid that they will look in vain for relief from a government which has failed after four years to implement the recommendations of the Duncan report with regard to coal and steel. These workingmen will have to wait because of their failure to provide adequate protection to our industries, particularly to shipbuilding. A remedy can hardly be expected from a government which lacks solidarity and which is so diversified with regard to its fiscal policy. That remedy will be lacking so long as we have a prime minister who holds such narrow views as were displayed when he told this house and this country that he would not allow his government to give a single five cent piece to any province which had a Tory premier.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have decided at this late moment to take part in this discussion because of some of the speeches to which I have listened to-night. Perhaps I am in a happier situation than the majority of the members of this House of Commons, for I represent a constituency which has enjoyed more prosperity during the last two years than at any period since confederation.
The situation which has been depicted with so much gloom by our Conservative friends is but a temporary one. Considerable improvement had taken place during the season of 1929 when compared with the conditions which existed in 1921, when this government took over the reins of office. During the summer season of 1929 this country enjoyed the greatest era of prosperity that it had known since confederation. Never in the history of this nation have we enjoyed greater prosperity, greater development and greater contentment, and nowhere else in the world could a labouring class be found who enjoyed a higher standing of living than did the people of Canada during the year 1929. A reaction occurred late in the fall arising from conditions over which no government could have control. Shortly after that reaction occurred ws were told by the leading financiers, bankers and industrialists, both in the public press and elsewhere, that Canada was enjoying the greatest prosperity of any civilized country in the world. The causes of that reaction are known to every hon. member on the other side of the house. The main cause was the inability to .move the wheat crop of 1929, an abnormal situation for which no government could make provision. That situation was

Unemployment-Mr. Lapierre
intensified by the stock market crash which occurred in the United States, another cause which could not be foreseen or prevented. This condition arose during our period of seasonal unemployment and it will disappear within the course of the next few months. I am sure that our Conservative friends dread to see the result of the Liberal policy as it will apply to conditions in Canada after this temporary period of depression.
We have heard a great deal about the situation in the United States as well as in Canada, but I think the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) has depicted a situation which should give more concern to hon. members than the temporary condition now existing in this country. The unemployment in Canada is not to be compared with the unemployment which prevails in every other part of the world. I have before me an article which appeared in the Literary Digest of March 29, in which conditions in other parts of the world are clearly set forth. This article shows quite definitely that the conditions in other countries are much worse than those in Canada. The article, which is entitled A World of the Workless, reads as follows:
In every big industrial country of the world the tragic tide of unemployment is said to be rising rapidly.
A few years ago, we are told, it was estimated that the total of unemployed was 20,000,000. The figure now is believed to be nearly 30,000,000. So declares the London Daily Herald, a labour organ and the official newspaper of the Labour party.
Recent reports from America and Germany, it adds, coupled with the serious situation in Britain, have emphasized the fact that the crisis extends over the globe.
Japan is no exception, for business depression is widespread there, factories are shutting down, and this newspaper continues:
"A short time ago the late government estimated the total workless at 300,000. To-day the figure exceeds 800,000, and it is forecast that the million mark will quickly be passed.
Labour organizations in Japan are drafting remedial measures, and the government is preparing a scheme of unemployment insurance.
As in Japan, so elsewhere. The latest estimates of the unemployed in the United States vary, but some put the total at the enormous figure of 6.000,000.
Mr. William Green, president of the American Federation of Labour, says the 'danger point' has been reached. He declares that 22 per cent of organized labour is idle, and that 43 per cent of the building workers are out of work."
If we turn to Europe, the Daily Herald goes on to say, we find a similar condition. At the end of December, it informs us, Germany had
4,583,000	idle organized workers.
During a week in February, it is pointed out, no fewer than 30,000 were added to the Germans receiving unemployment benefit. We read then:
[Mr. Lapierre. 3
, "Italy, whose industrial activity is comparatively small, has nearly half a million workers recorded as unemployed.
France is the only known exception among countries which have large-scale industry, though here the peculiar circumstances make comparison difficult."
I wish to call the attention of some of my hon friends to the peculiar situation existing in France at the present time:
"No recent figures are available for Russia, the latest were for October, 1928, when nearly two millions of the 11,000,000 organized workers were idle.
Claims have been made that industry in Russia will absorb 5,000,000 new workers in the next two years, but that is not fact but prophecy."
Economists have suggested that the unemployment was temporary, and that when the world has settled down to postwar conditions, production and trade would right themselves. That view is now discredited, and the outlook is regarded with apprehension.
That depicts the worldwide situation at the present moment with regard to labour, leaving Canada in a far better industrial and financial position than any other country in the civilized world.
We have heard a great deal about conditions in the United States. Some of my hon. friends on the other side, using the old familiar slogan, were still harping on Canadians leaving to go to the United States. I am now quoting from the same periodical, the Literary Digest of March 22 of this year, as follows:
Washington reports two elderly women, a policeman and half a dozen demonstrators hurt, and thirteen persons arrested when police used tear gas and blackjacks to suppress a riot which followed a Communist demonstration in front of the White House.
Cleveland reports more than 100 injured by flying police-clubs when "a cursing, jeering crowd of 10,000" battled several hundred police "after a Communist unemployment demonstration had been conducted without violence of any kind."
Detroit reports fourteen persons, including one policeman, sent to hospitals, and thirty-one arrested when mounted police prevented an unemployment rally.
Pittsburgh reports five men sent to hospitals, severely beaten, and twelve arrested when a Communist parade broke up in a riot.
Milwaukee reports forty-two men and youths arrested when police intervened in a demonstration by 1,500 unemployed men, and then raided Communist headquarters.
Seattle reports one man injured, and twelve arrested when police dispersed a crowd of 500, led by Communists.
Buffalo reports four Communist speakers arrested when they refused to leave Lafayette square, where a Red demonstration had been planned.

Unemployment-Mr. Robinson
New Haven reports police thwarted three attempts by a group of Communists to storm the city hall to present an employment petition to the mayor.
Chicago, Philadelphia, and San Francisco report Communist parades held without disorder.
That is the situation into which a high protective tariff has brought the United States, and had the same policy been put into force in Canada a similar condition would have been created here. But what I have been quoting so far has been from United States periodicals. I will now quote from the Standard of March 22 in which are given the results of an interview with R. W. Gould, Secretary of the Canadian Manufacurers' Association. The article, which is headed "Conditions are bad in States, says R. W. Gould," reads:
Conditions in the United States after the had break last fall improved, but another set back has occurred from which a slow recovery is now being made, reported R. W. Gould, secretary of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, in an interview with The Standard this morning upon his return from New York and Boston. Mass.
Undoubtedly, he said, a great deal of unemployment exists and there have been frequent demonstrations by the jobless.
Mr. Gould surveyed the general industrial position and found a far from happy situation in a number of cases. For instance, at Boston, lie heard that the cotton trade is in a pretty bad way with many mills closing down with the intention of reopening in the south.
The boot and shoe situation is also very unsatisfactory, he said. The trade is hard hit by competition from Czechoslovakia, he added. Strangely enough this competition is caused largely by Americans who obtained their experience in Boston and have gone to Slovakia and opened plants there. Labour is cheap and they are pressing hard the American home producers.
The outlook is bad also in the silk and hosiery industries, declared Mr. Gould. This is due largely, he commented, to the disorganized condition of the industries themselves.
The fishing industry, he found, has been fairly steady with both catches and markets good. Some 14 new super trawlers are being built he ascertained and will be launched in the next few months. The Americans, he added, have an eye on the Canadian market.
The tariff situation, he stated, is very disturbing.
In view of the situation, which prevails in Washington at present, are we Liberals not justified in claiming for the Liberal party a policy that has at least maintained a certain amount of prosperity and avoided the grave condition now existing in the United States? Has not the policy which the Liberal party enunciated at its convention in 1919 been carried out to the extent of giving us the most prosperous era this country has ever experienced?
In view of those facts, difficult as our situation is at the present time, I feel that the government is fully able to cope with it, and the people of Canada who realize this condition of affairs will see to it, when the time comes, that the government are returned to power with a larger majority than they at present have in the house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this late stage of the debate I will not detain the house very long, but the unemployment situation in the border cities is,
I believe, more acute in proportion to popula-lation than in any other part of Canada; and we also have an international labour situation. One reason why we have so many unemployed in the winter season I trace back to 1926 when the government changed the duties on automobiles. By its action it forced the automobile industry to adopt United States methods of -mass production. Let me illustrate what I mean. If a company planned to manufacture 30,000 cars they would order all their materials; when ready to start they would employ three shifts, each working eight hours a day, push forward the work as quickly as possible, then lay off two shifts and keep the remaining shift going for three days a week. That has been the situation in the border cities for the last two years; indeed some of the industries practically closed up. This means throwing out of employment
5,000	to 6,000 men. We have another situation in regard to which I cannot do better than quote a paragraph from the Border Cities Star of January 30 of this year. It says:
Our greatest difficulty, of course, lies in the fact that the border cities seem to be a mecca for a large part of all the unemployed men in Canada. This is due, probably, to two or three factors. We are widely known as the centre of the Canadian automotive industry, and the automotive industry, it is just as well known, pays attractive wages. Secondly, our community lias had an unusually rapid progress and the news of our expansion has travelled everywhere. Thirdly, we are next door to the United States, and large numbers of people come here from Europe and from all over Canada with the idea of eventually getting across the line. While they are here, of course, they clog the local labour market.
Our charitable institutions and our towns and cities are taxed to the utmost in taking care of the unemployed during the winter. We have down there the Good Fellows, who raise a very large sum every year to take care of the poor. The city of Windsor also spends a large amount each year for the same purpose. In January last the city was taking care of 400 families, providing them with groceries, milk and fuel.

Unemployment-Mr. Robinson
I claim that under such conditions they may reasonably expect some help from the federal government because of the fact that these conditions are caused by the bringing into this country of immigrants by the federal government, and by the change of tariff in the automobile industry which the government made in 1926.
I would urge upon the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) and the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) that they be very careful how they handle the situation on the border. For instance, an order in council was passed on the 7th day of August last, one paragraph of which provides that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization may admit any contract labourer if satisfied that his labour or services are required in Canada. The principle seems to be entirely right, but in practice it is not always followed. For instance, if the combination lock of a safe or vault cannot be opened and an expert has to be called in from Detroit, when he comes over with his tools he is turned back by the immigration officer. Only the other day a man came over from Detroit to do some work for the Ford Motor Company. He had his tools with him, and he was refused admittance into this country. The result was that it was broadcast from a Detroit radio station that night that one American who was going over to Canada to do a day's work had been turned back at the border, and it was pointed out that 8.000 Canadians crossed the border daily to work in Detroit. Many institutions in Detroit are only looking for an opportunity to dismiss Canadians and employ Americans. Let me quote from a letter that I received in this connection from Windsor:
Jerry Buckley (Station WMBC) announced over the radio that an American citizen who had obtained a job with the Ford Motor Company of Canada, on bringing his tools over to go to work, was not allowed to proceed but was turned back to the United States. One of the immigration officers at this port on being asked the question, how they handle these matters, if an American citizen came to Windsor to seek work, stated he would be turned back immediately. In view of the fact that 8,000 Canadians cross the border every day and work in Detroit, and only a few Americans work in this country, think it very inadvisable to follow this policy of turning American citizens back. Think it will do us more harm than good.
That letter was dated the 15th of March. He writes again on the 20th of March, on the letterhead of the Ford Motor Company:
Will say that I am vitally interested in this as I work in Detroit and the matter was called to my attention where I worked, that I had a lot of nerve coming over there and working when their citizens are not allowed to secure 
work in Windsor. I do not know how you feel about the matter, but if you feel as I do, hope you will take this matter up with the Minister of Immigration.
Then he goes on to say:
With 8,000 Canadians crossing the border every day and working in Detroit, I think it rather foolish to keep any American citizens from securing work in Windsor. If they can get work here they are smarter than I am, as I have never been able to get work here, and I take my hat off to any man who can get work here.
(Signed) M. C. McCullough.
I know that our immigration laws have to be carried out, but to my mind this regulation with regard to contract labour should apply only to numbers of men who are brought over on contract, because occasions often arise when an expert is required in connection with the installation of machinery or something of that kind, and there can be no objection to allowing such a man to enter for a day's work or so.
Now I want to show the other side of the case. It is the case of a man who worked with the Hudson-Essex motor car company for four and a half years in Detroit. He was an inspector, and he was discharged because he lived in Windsor and could not produce American citizenship papers. He receives a notice to report at the employment office, and I have here a copy of his discharge certificate, as reproduced in the Border Cities Star of April 1, 1930. It shows that his ability and deportment were good, and that his last operation was working as an inspector. I might point out that 16,000 Hudson-Essex motor cars were shipped into Canada during the past year, valued at least at $15,000,000 I think it a very short-sighted policy on the part of any company doing that much business in Canada to discharge a few Canadians who might be working in their plant at Detroit. As far as doing any work on their cars on this side of the line is concerned, they do not even put Canadian air in the tires. I remember that in 1928 I drew to the attention of the then Minister of Finance a statement that he made in the house in 1926, to the effect that the change made in the tariff at that time would force these motor companies to manufacture in Canada. The opposite has been the case so far as the Hudson motor company is concerned. I should like to put on Hansard this article from the Border Cities Star of April 1, 1930:
Hudson-Essex Man is Fired Because He Lives In Canada, A. G. Guest Is Informed
Off Roll For Good
Must Move to Detroit And Become U. S.
Citizen To Get Consideration Refuting statements of the Hudson Motor Car Company of Detroit that it was showing

Unemployment-Mr. Ladner
no discrimination in laying off Canadian workers, E. Grant Guest, who lives on highway No. 3 near Windsor, to-day stated that he had been told his services were no longer wanted because he was a Canadian.
First Notice March 15
Mr. Guest after working almost continunously for the Hudson company since August 4, 1925, was summarily ordered to report to the company employment office on March 15. "Report to the employment office with citizenship papers," the notice stated.
As Mr. Guest explained to the employment office officials, he had no citizenship papers and had not moved to Detroit as he had no previous notice.
"I explained the situation to Mr. Tholl, one of the men in the employment office, and after I had done so he concluded the interview by saying, 'That will be all,'" Mr. Guest declared. "The next day with no warning I received a notice that I was being laid off."
The notice which Mr. Guest brought to The Star office stated the reason for termination of his employment was "Readjustment of working force to provide work for Detroiters."
Superiors Regretful
Mr. Guest said the foreman and other immediate superiors were indignant at the treatment lie received but knowing the futility of any attempt to keep him on the payroll did not dare to make an open protest to the motor company executives.
"There are five other men I know of in the same predicament," Mr. Guest explained. "It means that after working five years to learn the Hudson method of doing things 1 am thrown out of a job with less chance of getting another position than if I had not been a steady worker and had floated from one plant to another."
Mr. Guest said he had not worked for any other company since going to work for the Hudson organization almost five years ago. He said that he had worked for five months in the old l'aige factory in Detroit before working for the Hudson company.
"On March 15 I went to see Mr. Holmwood in charge of employment, but he told me that I would never be reemployed as long as I lived in Canada," Mr. Guest said. "I was told that not only would I have to live in Detroit but would have to have first citizenship papers before I could be reemployed. I asked if it would be possible that in event of improved business conditions within three or four years if I could be re-hired, and Mr. Holmwood said that if it came to the place where the company was forced to go out and hire men in the streets, my reemployment might be considered, but as the order stood at present it was impossible to employ me."
Passes Up Detroit
Mr. Guest, who is 31 years old and married, said that he had made efforts to obtain employment in Border Cities plants without success, but had not endeavored to find another job in Detroit as he felt it would be futile in view of the orders there not to hire any Canadians, and also because of the few men being hired. He worked in the Jefferson plant of the Hudson Company as a paint inspector in the body trimming department when let out, but when the Hudson company was working three
production lines instead of two as at present he was a gang work leader. On his card stating he had been dismissed he was credited with "good" ability and deportment, the highest ranking possible.
Mr. Guest said he did not know what he could do for employment. Counting on his work with the Hudson company as permanent he had not made any previous plans to work elsewhere.
Another serious feature of the unemployment in the border cities is that hundreds and hundreds of men have lost their homes, some that were half paid for; in fact in many cases it is the second home that they have lost. Many industries to-day will not hire men over 40 to 45 years of age, their excuse being that the compensation act forces them to do this. This means that in a few years we shall have a serious problem on our hands in connection with old age pensions or unemployment insurance. I would strongly urge the government to take steps to help out the situation, at least next year, if they cannot do so this year. The federal authorities collect a handsome revenue in Windsor, the excise and customs amounting to over $30,000.000' for the past twelve months, and the post office receipts $386,000. In view of this, and of the fact that unemployment in the border cities is not altogether due to local causes over which the municipalities might have control, I think the government should deal with the situation as a national problem.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF ME. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few observations on this matter because of its vast importance to the lives and happiness of so man}'' people throughout Canada, a considerable number of whom reside in my constituency. We have all had occasion, unfortunately, to witness the difficulties of many of our working people in their efforts to find employment. It is a pitiable condition of life, and it appeals to me in particular because of its human side. I have had men come into my office in Vancouver whom I have known for years to be in regular employment, honest, respectable men, seeking an honest day's work. These men are the victims of the economic depression through which the country is passing, and it seems to me that there does devolve on the government a responsibility which they cannot escape.
The question before parliament is, what has the government done to meet that responsibility? Has the government done anything? We have been presented with an impressive array of statistical data, we have heard ingenious arguments, and the government and its supporters have even tried to convince us that there is no unemployment in the country.

Unemployment-Mr. Ladner
But notwithstanding the data and arguments, we all realize that there is an appalling amount of unemployment throughout the Dominion. It may be said that unemployment is a worldwide condition, and to some extent this is true. We know that the economic pendulum swings alternately from prosperity to depression and back again to prosperity, and in my opinion it is incumbent on governments to provide for the periods of depression so that those least able to help themselves may be tided over until the pendulum does swing back to prosperity.
We have heard several solutions offered to deal with this problem of unemployment. I propose to deal only with one of those solutions-unemployment insurance. Unemployment insurance would help the victim of world conditions, with the creation of which he has had nothing to do but for which he suffers acutely, to provide the necessaries of life for his wife and family, to feed and clothe them, and thus mitigate their sufferings until there is another period of prosperity in which he will be able to participate. I was very much interested the other evening-and I take this occasion to remark upon the matter because I had something to do with it-I was very much interested, nay, I was astonished, to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggest a denial of his assertion on a former occasion, that the old age pension scheme involved a vicious principle. It happened that I asked the question when he. was speaking on another subject, but I wish to reassert what is contained in Hansard; it shows that the Prime Minister did say that the granting of money for old age pensions was a vicious principle. We need have no doubt upon that question, because Hansard records it in clear, cold print.
I think the most amazing statement in the annals of statesmanship and political history in this country was made the other day when the Prime Minister gave utterance to a statement of political depravity which is surpassed only by his lack of policy on the question of unemployment. He told us that he was not disposed to make contributions to Tory governments in Canada. It seems to me that the function of a party in power is to govern the country and to formulate public policies; it is not the duty of a government to assume that extreme degree of partisanship which causes its leader, the Prime Minister, to tell the Canadian public that if any section of the people fail to carry out the partisan political policies which he has dictated, it will be incumbent upon him, as a Mussolini or a man of similar dictatorial powers, to punish

them because they happen to desire a political party of different persuasion. It should not be the policy of the federal government to punish provinces by refusing to cooperate with them financially on matters which would merit the favourable consideration of an ordinary prime minister and government.
With respect to the question before the house, I may tell hon. members that I have taken the opportunity to read the budget debates, and particularly the speeches of the Prime Minister from 1922 up to the present time, in connection with the various budgets presented. So far as fiscal policies are concerned one can find in those speeches the most inconsistent statements it is possible to conceive. The net result of the observations by the Prime Minister in years gone by is that his fiscal policy exists for the producers and the consumers, but as far as I have been able to ascertain, if you eliminated from Canada the producers and the consumers you would not have many people left. In his speech on the budget in 1928 the Prime Minister placed on record an extended list of reductions in the tariff. This list, which covers a great number of pages in Hansard, was placed by the Prime Minister at the end of his speech as a sort of addendum. Now, I find it most significant that at the present time we have a powerful factor in this cabinet in the person of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), who is a declared low tariff man. We have the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who formerly sounded "(the death knell of protection;" but it is to be noted that that bell has not been sounded during more recent sessions. There is the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) who is a declared free trader. There is our friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Crerar); out of consideration for the Prime Minister I will not refer to the speeches of the Minister of Railways while he was leader of the Progressive party. The hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred constitute a very powerful circle in the government forces. They are declared free traders or low tariff men, and in my opinion part of the difficulty in regard to unemployment has been brought about by the government being wedded to a theory rather than concerned about the exigencies of business conditions. This condition exists to such an extent that in our trade with the United States we are buying from them $900,000,000 worth of goods per year, mostly manufactured products. We are selling them raw products to the extent of $500,000,000 per year. Those hon. members who analyze the trade statistics of Canada will find a very interest-

Unemployment-Mr. Ladner
ing situation. I refer to this matter at the present time because I anticipated that the Prime Minister and his colleagues will proceed to Great Britain to attend the economic conference, unless the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) attends in his place, which of course depends upon the Prime Minister's decision as to an election. In view of the coming conference it may be interesting to know that since confederation we have sold to Great Britain, in excess of what we have purchased, the enormous figure of $5,800,000,000 worth of goods, but we have purchased from the United States in excess of our sales to them, the enormous amount of $5,400,000,000 worth of goods. The attitude of the Prime Minister and his government is that they shall reduce their tariff rates, that they shall allow more manufactured goods from the United States to enter this country and to displace industries, thereby depriving Canadian working people of occupations in which they might otherwise be engaged. The outcome of the next election is something to which hon. gentlemen on this side of the house are looking forward with considerable interest. It is said that the Prime Minister is framing a protectionist budget. I do not know how my hon, friend the Minister of the Interior would greet such a situation, neither do I know how it would affect other members of the cabinet. Conditions in this country in respect to industry and unemployment are such that a protectionist budget is the one thing that would help Canada. I do not believe, however, that it will be the Prime Minister and his government that will bring in such a policy; I believe it will be the hon. gentleman who is at present leader of the opposition, as the head of the government in Canada.
